studies.title: Made Firm Then Set Out
studies.meaning: The opening makes two claims about the Book in a single clause: its verses were made firm, then set out in detail. Commentators read the pair as a sequence, an unbreakable core that is afterwards unfolded into commands, histories and arguments, though some take the first verb to mean secured against contradiction and others to mean fixed in wording. The purpose follows at once, that you worship none but God, and the speaker introduces himself twice over, as warner and as bearer of good news.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years of the mission, in a run of surahs that open with disconnected letters and turn quickly to the histories of earlier prophets. Opposition in the city had hardened past argument into ridicule and pressure on the weakest followers. The surah answers by putting the Book's own credentials first, before it tells a single story.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to restrain, the same root behind the words for wisdom and judgement. It suggests a text held so tightly together that nothing can be worked loose from it, before any explaining begins.
The root means to separate joint from joint. The intensive form pictures a book articulated into distinct parts, each one distinguishable, rather than delivered as a single undivided mass.
The pair is ordered deliberately. Warning comes first because the audience is being addressed about a danger, but the sentence is allowed to finish on the good news rather than the threat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on the spoken word. Poetry was performed at seasonal fairs and judged line by line, and a strong composition could travel the peninsula within a season. Merchants sealed agreements by oath rather than by paper, and a man's standing rested on whether his speech held up under repetition. A claim that a text had been made firm and then explained was a claim these listeners knew how to test.
studies.didYouKnow: Five surahs open with the letters Alif, Lam, Ra: this one, Jonah, Joseph, Abraham and al-Hijr. All five are Meccan and all five carry long prophet narratives. They sit in two runs, chapters ten to twelve and fourteen to fifteen, separated only by the surah that opens with Alif, Lam, Meem, Ra.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is given a structure before it is given a message: firm, then differentiated, from a source named as Wise and Informed. The two names answer two separate doubts, that the Book might be arbitrary and that it might be uninformed about the people it addresses. What follows, worship of God alone, is then not one instruction among many but the thing the whole architecture exists to deliver.

crossReferences.why: Describes a scripture with the same verb of detailed exposition, given in Arabic for people who know.
Opens the preceding surah with the same letters and a comparable claim about a wise Book.
States as a purpose of creation the very thing this opening names as the point of revelation.

studies.applyIt: Read the first two ayat of this surah slowly, then read its final ayah, and notice that the chapter ends where it began, on worship and reliance. Between them lie six prophets and four ruined towns. Today, when something you are reading gets long, try holding its opening line in mind and see what the middle looks like from there.

studies.title: Until A Stated Term
studies.meaning: Two verbs arrive in order: seek forgiveness, then turn back. The classical commentators take the sequence seriously, clearing what lies behind before facing forward, and they read the promised good enjoyment as a decent rather than lavish share of this life, running to a term already fixed. The further grace given to every possessor of merit is understood as a return proportioned to effort. The alternative is put without threat language, only turning away and a day the speaker says he fears for them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a city grown wealthy on the caravan trade and inclined to hear the message as a threat to it. What is promised for repentance here is worldly as well as final, which commentators connect to the standing objection that following this man would cost a family its livelihood. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: The form asks for something rather than performing it. The root covers covering over and shielding, so what is requested is that a fault be covered, not that it be argued away or forgotten.
The verb is physical before it is moral: to return to a place you left. Repentance in this word is a change of direction, not only regret about the direction already taken.

The noun means what you use and then leave behind, like travelling goods. Joining it to the word for good keeps the promise modest, a sufficient and decent enjoyment, explicitly bounded by a stated term.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan household measured security in stored dates, water rights, and a share in the winter and summer caravans. Debt was ordinary, and one bad season could hand a family's independence to a creditor. A promise of decent provision until a stated term spoke to people who knew that every arrangement they had, a lease, a truce, a loan, ran to a date that somebody had set.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered here as ask your Lord for forgiveness, then repent to Him, occurs three times in this surah and nowhere else in the Quran: in this opening address, then in the mouth of Hud to his people, and again in the mouth of Shuaib. Salih says the same thing a few ayat earlier with the two verbs joined slightly differently.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is placed before provision, which reverses the order most people assume. The passage does not say that repenting buys prosperity; it says the two belong to a single generosity, and that both run until a term God has already set. Naming Him Capable of all things at the close removes the last hedge, since the return being described is not a possibility to weigh but a settled fact.

crossReferences.why: Noah makes his people the same offer: seek forgiveness, and rain, wealth and children follow.
Hud repeats this formula to Aad word for word, with rain and added strength as what is promised.
Names God as Forgiver of sins and Accepter of repentance in the same breath as severity.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order. Most of us try to improve first and apologise afterwards, if at all. For one thing you have been meaning to put right, reverse it today: name the fault to God plainly, with no plan attached and nothing promised, and only then start thinking about what would have to change. See whether the second part comes any easier.

studies.title: What The Chest Is Holding
studies.meaning: A gesture is described and then quietly dismantled. People fold their chests inward and pull cloth over themselves, and the ayah lets that picture stand for a moment before saying that concealment and disclosure arrive equally. Commentators differ on the gesture itself, some reporting it as literal avoidance of the recitation, others reading it as an image for hostility kept private. Either way, the closing clause moves past behaviour altogether to what a chest contains.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical reports connect the ayah to men who turned away and drew their cloaks over their heads when the Quran was recited near the sanctuary, so as not to be seen listening. The reports vary in their details, and the commentators present them as illustrations of the described behaviour rather than as one fixed occasion of revelation.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to bend a thing back on itself. Used of a chest it pictures a person curling inward, and the same root supplies the ordinary Arabic words for two and for a fold.
The form carries seeking: they want the covering and go after it. This is the deliberate pulling of a garment up over the head, not the ordinary condition of being clothed.
A recurring phrase for the interior of a person. It names not thoughts as such but whatever the chest is holding, including things its owner has never put into words.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The cloak was the most private thing a person owned in Mecca. It served as coat, blanket and screen, and pulling it over the head was how you slept, mourned, or shut out a conversation you did not want. In a city where houses stood close and everyone's business was half public, a garment drawn up was the nearest thing to a door you could close.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered they wrap their chests occurs in this form only here in the whole Quran. Its root is otherwise everywhere in Arabic, supplying the words for two, for a pair, and for a bend in a road, but the image of a chest doubled over on itself is used once and never repeated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates God's knowledge inside the person rather than around him, which changes what privacy can mean. Concealing and revealing are named together and given the same verb of knowing, so the distinction survives socially and disappears entirely before God. This is stated with no threat attached, which is why commentators read it as description of God rather than as warning about punishment.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same point as a choice that makes no difference: keep your speech secret or announce it.
Adds the darting of the eyes to what chests conceal, so even the glance is counted.
Uses the identical closing phrase about chests after a costly setback, of thoughts men kept to themselves.

studies.applyIt: Sit with something you have never said out loud to anyone, and say it to God in plain words, as information rather than as confession. Nothing is being disclosed that He did not already have. What changes is on your side: the small distance between what you carry privately and what you are willing to admit that you carry.

studies.title: Every Creature Has Its Portion
studies.meaning: The claim is universal, and it is phrased as an undertaking. There is no moving creature whose provision is not upon God. Early scholars are careful that the wording does not make God a debtor. It describes a responsibility He has taken on. Two further things are known, where the creature settles and where it is placed for keeping. The classical readings differ over whether these mean life and death, the womb and the grave, or simply dwelling and lodging.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the opening of a surah that will spend most of its length on communities destroyed for refusing their prophets. This verse stands before all of that. Early scholars note the placement. A statement about provision for every creature is set at the head of a surah about collapse. The audience included people whose objection to the message was what following it would cost them.

keyTerms.note: What is given for sustenance rather than what is earned. The pronoun attaches it to the creature, so each has a portion described as already assigned to it rather than as a share of a common supply.
A noun of place from the verb to settle. Early scholars read it as where a creature lives, and also as the womb, so the word covers both a lifetime's ground and the first one it occupied.
From the verb to entrust something for safekeeping. It suggests a temporary holding rather than a home, which is why the classical readings of it include the grave.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anxiety about provision was seasonal and concrete. Rain arriving late meant thin animals and a hungry winter. Everyone had watched a family slide from enough to dependence in a single bad year. Wild animals were observed closely by people who lived alongside them. The fact that creatures with no stores and no plans were fed anyway was an observation. It was available to anyone outdoors.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a moving creature appears here and in a verse at 6:38 with a strikingly similar structure. Each makes a universal claim about animals. One says they are communities like you. This one says their provision has been undertaken. Read together, the two give the animal world a standing and a guarantee in almost identical grammar.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is described as an undertaking rather than a handout, which changes the worry it addresses. The question is not whether enough exists. It is whether anyone has taken it on. The answer is given before any human being is mentioned in the surah. Including every creature makes the claim testable by watching. The closing reference to a clear record ties provision to knowledge rather than to chance.

crossReferences.why: Points at creatures that carry no provision with them and are fed regardless.
Places provision in the heaven, along with what is being promised.
Makes the parallel claim about animals, calling them communities like your own.

studies.applyIt: Name the specific figure or the specific month that your anxiety about money actually attaches to. Write it down. Then notice that the verse does not promise plenty. It names a responsibility that has been taken on. The difference between those two is most of what makes the anxiety loud.
studies.explainEasier: Every living thing that moves on the earth is fed by God. He knows where each one lives and where it rests. All of it is written in a clear book.

studies.title: The Throne Upon The Waters
studies.meaning: Creation is given a purpose clause, and the purpose turns out to be a test of conduct rather than of belief or of quantity. The wording is best in deed, not most in deed, and the commentators hold to that: quality is what is being measured. Between the six days and the purpose sits a detail, the Throne standing over water, which the classical exegetes report without speculating past it. Then the reaction to resurrection is quoted, and it is not an argument but the word for sorcery.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when the raising of the dead was the one point on which the city's leadership would not move. Trade, poetry and pilgrimage continued unchanged whether or not a man was raised from dust, and the objection recorded here is not reasoned at all. Calling the claim witchcraft was a way of closing a conversation rather than entering it.

keyTerms.gloss: so that He may test you
keyTerms.note: The verb is used of trying a thing to find out its quality, as a garment is worn to see how it wears. What is named is the discovery of what a person is, not information God was lacking.
The comparative is one of excellence, not of amount. Classical commentators gloss it as the most sincere and the most correct action, which is why the phrase resists being turned into a tally.
The word for a raised seat of authority. Commentators describe the Throne as the greatest created thing and decline to picture it, treating the water beneath it as reported rather than explained.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the measure of everything in Arabia. A well decided where a tribe camped, which land was worth defending, and which routes a caravan could take, and the right to draw from one was inherited and fought over. Hearing that the Throne had stood over water before there was an earth put the most contested resource these listeners knew at the very beginning of the world.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase best in deed occurs four times in the Quran, and in three of them it names the purpose of something created: this ayah about the heavens and the earth, the ornaments of the earth at 18:7, and the making of death and life at 67:2. Each time the measure given is quality of action, never quantity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Giving creation a purpose clause turns the universe into an examination room rather than a display. Two things follow. The measure is conduct, which is available to anyone whatever else they were given, and the test is of quality, which cannot be gamed by volume. The mention of the Throne, left deliberately unexplained, marks the limit of what the passage is prepared to say about God's own situation.

crossReferences.why: Gives death and life the same stated purpose, testing which of you is better in conduct.
Says the earth's ornaments were made precisely as a test of the same quality of action.
Pairs the six days with the Throne again, adding night pursuing day in rapid succession.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you will do today that you already do regularly, a meal you cook, a message you answer, a task at work. Do that single one with more care than it strictly needs, and notice how much of your ordinary effort is aimed at getting through rather than at doing well. The gap is small, and it is the entire subject of this ayah.

studies.title: What Holds It Back
studies.meaning: A delay is imagined, and the response to it is predicted. Given more time the objection would not be dropped but sharpened into a taunt: what is keeping it. The answer comes as a change of tense and a change of verb. On the day it reaches them nothing turns it aside, and the thing they had made jokes about closes in around them. Commentators notice that the mockery itself is what encircles them, not merely a consequence of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demand to see the threatened punishment actually arrive is recorded again and again in this period, and the city's leadership treated its non-arrival as proof of nothing to answer. This surah is replying to that argument at length, since every prophet narrative that follows is a case where the delay ran long and the ending came anyway.

keyTerms.note: The first word usually means a community; here it carries an older sense of a period. Pairing it with counted insists that the delay has a number attached, known to whoever set it.
A verb used of penning livestock and of damming water. The taunt imagines the punishment as something being physically restrained, which concedes rather more than the speakers intend.
Used in the Quran of a consequence encircling the people who produced it. It suggests a ring drawn tight from all sides rather than a blow arriving from somewhere outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan life ran on obligations with dates attached. A loan was taken against the return of the summer caravan, a blood payment settled by an agreed season, a truce held until a named month. Asking what is holding something back was the ordinary language of a creditor whose term had passed, and everyone listening knew what it meant when an account finally came due.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated closed in appears about nine times in the Quran, and in every one of them it describes a consequence returning on the people who produced it, usually the very thing they had mocked. It is never used of an ordinary siege or an attack from outside, which is why translators reach for words like encompass and engulf.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is presented as a decision rather than an absence, which disposes of the argument that nothing happening means nothing will happen. The passage also makes ridicule consequential in itself. What they treated as a joke is the very thing that surrounds them, so the mockery is not punished by something separate; it becomes the shape the punishment takes.

crossReferences.why: Says the same of earlier messengers: what the mockers ridiculed was what closed in on them.
Records the identical demand to hurry the punishment, and answers that it will arrive suddenly.
Meets the request for haste by resetting the scale, a day with your Lord against a thousand years.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you were given long ago that has not yet come true, about your health, your work, or a relationship you have been coasting on. Notice how the passing time has quietly turned itself into your evidence that the warning was wrong. Name that to yourself in one sentence today, without arguing either side of it.

studies.title: Troubles Have Gone Away From Me
studies.meaning: Two symmetrical failures are set out, and neither is the obvious one. Loss produces not sorrow but despair joined to ingratitude, as though the good that had been given was never real. Gain produces not relief but a claim, troubles have gone away from me, said as if they had left of their own accord. Commentators point out that the second state is the more dangerous of the two, because it feels like happiness and arrives with no sense of anything having gone wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed to a merchant society whose fortunes rose and fell with the caravan seasons. The description is of the human being in general rather than of any group, and the exception granted in the following ayah confirms that reading. No occasion of revelation is reported; the commentators treat the pair as a portrait of character before it has been formed.

keyTerms.note: The verb is of tasting rather than eating. It marks both the mercy and the prosperity as samples rather than possessions, which is exactly what the person receiving them fails to register.
An intensive form, considerably stronger than the ordinary word for losing hope. It names despair as a settled disposition rather than a mood that passes once a loss is absorbed.
Also intensive. The root concerns display, so the fault named is not private satisfaction at good fortune but the impulse to hold that fortune up for other people to see.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trader's whole year could turn on one caravan. Loss meant more than money, since a man who could not meet his obligations lost standing among people who would remember it for a generation, while a single good season put him in a position to lend rather than to borrow. The two states described here were not abstractions in Mecca. The city watched families move between them.
studies.didYouKnow: The same swing is described three times in the Quran with almost the same vocabulary, here, at 17:83, and at greater length in 41:49 to 51. Each time it is placed among arguments about revelation rather than among moral instructions, which suggests the portrait is offered as evidence about people rather than as advice to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes ingratitude a failure of memory rather than of manners. In both halves the person loses track of where the good came from: in loss he concludes it was never given, and in gain he concludes it arrived by itself. Naming the pair before naming the exception establishes that the steady believer described next is not the natural human state but something worked for.

crossReferences.why: Draws out the same swing at length, and adds the further claim that this is mine by right.
Compresses both halves into one ayah: turning aside in ease, despairing when hardship touches.
Notes people rejoicing at mercy yet despairing at what their own hands have sent ahead.

studies.applyIt: The next time something goes right for you this week, catch the very first sentence you say about it. If it begins with the word I, or with finally, stop and add where you think it came from. You are not correcting a sin. You are checking whether your instinct still knows the difference between receiving and acquiring.

studies.title: Except Those Who Held Steady
studies.meaning: One short exception is set against the whole portrait before it. What breaks the pattern of despair and boasting is not temperament but two things done: holding steady, and acting well. Commentators take the order seriously, reading steadfastness as what makes right action possible when circumstances are pushing the other way. The reward is stated in two parts, a covering over of fault and something great whose content is not specified, and both are promised to the same people.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a passage on human instability that begins two ayat earlier. The believers being described were a small group under social pressure in a city where a family could withdraw its protection from a member and leave him exposed. Steadfastness in that setting meant staying visible rather than quietly withdrawing, which is why the ayah joins it at once to deeds.

keyTerms.note: The root is used of restraining an animal and of a fortress holding out. It covers waiting, but its centre is keeping a position under pressure rather than accepting whatever happens.
The root means to be sound or in working order, and it gives the ordinary word for repair. Good deeds in this vocabulary are actions that put something right, not simply actions that are allowed.
The first word is a workman's pay, earned and owed rather than given. Attaching an adjective of size instead of a description leaves the amount open while insisting the transaction is real.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wages in Mecca were often paid in kind and often paid late: a share of a caravan's return, a measure of dates after harvest, water rights for a season. A labourer worked on the strength of a promise from someone whose word he had no choice but to trust. Calling the hereafter a wage rather than a gift placed it in a category every hired man already understood.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact exception clause that opens this ayah occurs in only one other place in the Quran, at 41:35, and both times it does the same work: rescuing a group from a sweeping negative statement about people in general. In each case what qualifies them is endurance rather than any advantage they were born with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception comes after the diagnosis rather than before it, so the steady person is defined as someone who came out of the same material as everyone else. Forgiveness is named first, which implies that steadfastness is not the same as blamelessness; those who hold on still need covering. The reward's size is asserted while its content is withheld, and the classical commentators leave it there.

crossReferences.why: Makes a comparable exception against a general statement of loss, adding truth and patience.
Says that repelling evil with what is better is granted to nobody except those who persevere.
Lists the patient who pray, spend and repel evil with good among those given the final home.

studies.applyIt: Patience here is joined to doing, not to waiting. So take whatever you are currently enduring and find one small action inside it that would count as repair: a message you owe, a room you have stopped tidying, a person you have been short with lately. Do that one thing today without waiting for the situation itself to improve first.

studies.title: You Are Only A Warner
studies.meaning: The address turns to the Prophet and names a pressure rather than a failure. The opening particle is one of supposition, and commentators are careful with it: what is described is a temptation felt, not an omission committed. What tightens the chest is a demand for spectacle, a treasure or an accompanying angel, and the reply redefines the work. He delivers warning; the outcome belongs somewhere else. The final clause names God as the one entrusted with everything, which is where the weight gets put down.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the leadership had moved past argument into setting conditions: bring us a sign of the kind we specify. The demand for a treasure or a visible angel is recorded across several surahs of this period. Classical commentators read this ayah as consolation addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) rather than as any kind of rebuke.

keyTerms.note: A particle of supposition. It stops the sentence short of asserting that anything was left out, which is why commentators read the ayah as naming a pressure and heading it off rather than recording a fault.
From a root meaning narrowness. Arabic locates distress as a tightening of the chest, so the word gives the physical sensation of pressure rather than naming an emotion in the abstract.
A term from ordinary business: the agent you hand your affairs to and whose management you then rely on. Applied to God, it moves responsibility for results away from the messenger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Mecca an agent handled what an owner could not. A merchant travelling north left his affairs with someone empowered to sell, settle and collect, and the arrangement worked only if the owner then stopped second-guessing it. Naming God with that word told a man under sustained pressure that the results of his work were another party's business, contracted and no longer his to carry.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase rendered you are only a warner occurs once in the entire Quran, in this ayah. Related constructions appear elsewhere, such as you are only a reminder at 88:21, but the specific wording used to steady the Prophet against a demand for treasure and angels is not repeated anywhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line around what prophethood is. A messenger is accountable for delivering and not for persuading, which protects the message from being adjusted to demand and protects the messenger from carrying a burden he was never handed. That the strain is acknowledged at all, and in the second person, is itself part of the point: pressure is not treated as evidence of weak faith.

crossReferences.why: Names the same constriction of the chest at what they say, and answers it with praise.
Records the identical demand for a treasure and an accompanying angel, and gives the same answer.
States the limit plainly: you are a reminder, and you are not in control over them.

studies.applyIt: Find the part of a current worry that is genuinely yours to do, and write it down in one line. Then write the part that depends on other people, on timing, or on outcomes you cannot reach. Keep the first line somewhere you will see it tomorrow. The second one you can hand over; that is what this ayah tells someone under far more pressure than you.

studies.title: Then Bring Ten Chapters
studies.meaning: The accusation is quoted and met with an invitation rather than a defence. If the Book was composed, composition is a skill the objectors possess, so let them produce ten chapters of the same kind and bring in whatever help they can find. Commentators note the concession folded into the challenge: the ten need not even be true, only invented, which strips away every excuse except inability. The condition attached at the end concerns honesty, not outcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge that this was a fabrication is answered in several places with challenges of different sizes, and the commentators read them as a sequence addressed to an audience that took great pride in its eloquence. Mecca judged verse in public and knew exactly what producing a rival composition would involve, and no attempt is recorded from those years.

keyTerms.note: The root is used of cutting and stitching leather. The accusation is one of manufacture, pieces assembled into something that looks whole, which makes it a claim about craft rather than about sincerity.
The number is specified rather than left open, and the unit named is the chapter. The scale is set large enough to rule out one lucky line and small enough that the attempt is realistic.
The same root as the accusation, turned back on the challengers. It grants them permission to invent freely, narrowing the contest down to whether the thing can be done at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's literary culture was competitive and public. Poets performed at seasonal gatherings, tribes kept champions the way they kept horses, and a devastating verse could settle a quarrel that spears had not. Composition was not a private art in that world. Asking such a city for ten chapters was asking it to do in public the one thing it was proudest of.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran issues this challenge at four different scales, and they do not run in order of the Book. The whole of it is demanded at 17:88, ten chapters here, a single chapter at 10:38 and again at 2:23, and merely a discourse like it at 52:34. Commentators discuss the sequence and generally read the smaller demands as concessions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument offered is empirical rather than authoritative. Instead of asserting that the Book is from God, the passage names a test the objectors can run for themselves and stakes the claim on the result. That is a particular kind of confidence, and it also tells the reader what sort of thing the Quran takes itself to be: not merely true, but of a kind that cannot be counterfeited.

crossReferences.why: Reduces the same challenge to one chapter, with the same invitation to summon whatever helpers they have.
Raises it to the whole Book, and says humans and jinn together could not manage the like of it.
Places the single-chapter version directly after the identical accusation of invention.

studies.applyIt: Read a page of the Quran today, then read a page of something you consider very well written: a poem, an essay, a chapter of a novel you love. Do not rank them. Just notice how differently each one behaves, where it repeats, where it turns, what it does with an ending. The challenge in this ayah is asking for exactly that kind of attention.

studies.title: If They Do Not Answer
studies.meaning: The challenge is followed by its consequence. Failure to answer is not treated as a minor embarrassment but as evidence, and two conclusions are drawn from it: that the Book came down carrying God's own knowledge, and that there is no god but Him. Commentators observe that the addressee shifts inside the ayah, from believers who are told to know, to objectors who are asked a question. That question is left standing unanswered on the page.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, arriving immediately after the demand for ten invented chapters. Commentators read the two ayat as a single argument in two moves. They also note that no serious attempt to meet the challenge is recorded from the Meccan years, although the leadership had every motive to try and the poetic talent available to attempt it.

keyTerms.note: The form implies answering a call addressed to you. It is the same verb used of God answering prayer, so what is described is a failure to reply rather than only a refusal to compete.
The preposition carries accompaniment. Commentators read it as revelation sent down together with knowledge belonging to God, which is what marks it off from anything a person might assemble.
The root joins peace and handing over. The closing question asks whether, having run out of counter-arguments, they will now hand the matter over instead of continuing to hold it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab disputes had a recognised shape. A claim was made, a counter-claim invited, and if nobody answered, the silence itself was the verdict. Poets and orators lost standing in public by having nothing to say, and the loss was remembered. The ayah leans on that convention: in a culture where an unanswered challenge was a settled matter, an absent reply carried real weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who submit that ends this ayah is formed from the root that gives the religion its name, and in the whole of this long surah it appears only here. Across the Quran it is used far more often as a verb describing something a person does than as a label attached to a group.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An argument about a book is turned into a statement about God. If the text carries knowledge nobody could have supplied, then its source is singular, and the passage moves directly from that to the denial of any other god. The final question is put rather than pressed, leaving the reader to notice that the conclusion has already been reached and only the response is outstanding.

crossReferences.why: Says God Himself bears witness to what He revealed, and that He revealed it with His knowledge.
Sets a parallel test: bring a scripture from God with better guidance, if you are truthful.
Follows the same accusation with the observation that they deny what they never grasped.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you handle being out of arguments. Most people change the subject, get louder, or leave the room. The next time you are in a conversation where you realise you have nothing left to say and the other person is right, try saying exactly that, once, and see what it costs you. This ayah ends on a smaller version of the same question.

studies.title: Paid In Full Here
studies.meaning: The passage concedes a great deal before it withholds anything. Those who want this life and its ornament are paid in full, on time, with no shortfall, and the language used is that of an honest settlement rather than a swindle. What is denied is only what lies beyond it. Commentators generally read this of people whose intention terminates in the world, including those whose acts look religious, and they note that the second ayah cancels the works rather than punishing them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a city whose leading families measured standing in gold, imported cloth and reputation, and whose objection to the message was partly that it valued none of these. Commentators discuss whether the two ayat describe outright rejecters or anyone at all who acts for display, and they record both readings without settling between them.

keyTerms.note: The word means decoration added to a thing rather than the thing itself. Applied to worldly life it separates the life from the shine on it, and locates the desire squarely in the shine.
The verb is commercial, used of handing over less than the measure agreed. Denying it here insists the arrangement is honest: whatever was worked for is delivered without any deduction.
Used of an animal that grazes on something harmful and swells until it dies. The picture is not of a small return but of effort that looked like growth and turned out to be fatal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca kept its wealth visible. Standing was worn and displayed: imported cloth, worked silver, a good mount, the number of guests a household could feed through the pilgrimage season. Nobody buried gold and lived plainly. In that setting the word for ornament was not a metaphor, and full payment in this world meant precisely the thing people had arranged their lives to obtain.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as came to nothing is used in Arabic of livestock bloating fatally after grazing on fresh pasture. Classical lexicographers record that sense plainly, and it explains why the Quran's usual word for wasted deeds carries a suggestion of something that swelled impressively just before it failed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses the easy claim that worldly aims do not work. They do work, and they are paid. What is asserted instead is that a life aimed entirely at the visible receives exactly what it aimed at and nothing further, which makes the hereafter a question of intention rather than of accounting. Deeds are described as void rather than as debts, so the loss is of substance and not a sentence.

crossReferences.why: Sets the two harvests side by side: one is increased, the other given only in part here.
Contrasts what is hastened for whoever wants the fleeting life with what is striven for properly.
Names the greatest losers as people whose effort was wasted while they thought they were doing well.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you did this week that you would describe as good, and ask what you expected back from it. Not in order to condemn the answer, since most motives are mixed and mostly ordinary. Just find out whether the return you were quietly hoping for was something that could have arrived by the end of the week, or not.

studies.title: A Witness From Him
studies.meaning: A question is asked and its second half is left unspoken, so the comparison with the person just described has to be supplied by the listener. Three supports are stacked: clear evidence, a witness who recites it, and the Book of Moses standing behind both. Commentators differ sharply over the identity of that witness, some reading it as the angel of revelation, some as the Quran itself, some as a believing man, and they set the range out without deciding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that keeps returning to earlier scripture. The appeal to the Book of Moses reached an audience that knew the older revelations by report, through Jewish and Christian communities in Arabia and along the trade routes north. The factions are understood by the commentators as any assembled groups set against the message, whatever their own creed happened to be.

keyTerms.note: The word means something that makes a matter plain by itself. It is not proof assembled by argument but evidence whose own clarity does the work, which is why witnesses are stacked behind it rather than reasons.
Literally that which stands in front, and the word used for the one who leads a prayer. Applied to the Book of Moses it means a precedent placed ahead of what came after it.
A word for parties banded together. The plural keeps the opponents unnamed and various, so the sentence covers any grouping that sets itself against the message rather than one community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was how seventh-century Arabia settled anything at all. Land, marriage, debt and blood claims turned on who would stand up and say what they had seen, and a claim without a witness was barely a claim. Stacking evidence, then a reciting witness, then a book that came earlier, was speaking the language of a court that everyone listening had stood in.
studies.didYouKnow: The identity of the witness in this ayah is among the most discussed questions in classical commentary on the surah. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both lay several readings side by side without ruling, and the disagreement is not doctrinal but grammatical: it turns on which of the preceding nouns the pronoun is attached to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is presented here as continuous rather than new. Placing the Book of Moses before the present revelation makes the claim a historical one, that the same message has arrived again, and the earlier scripture is called a leader and a mercy rather than a superseded draft. The instruction that follows, to be in no doubt about it, is addressed to someone who already believes.

crossReferences.why: Names the Book of Moses a model and a mercy, with this one confirming it in the Arabic tongue.
Says those given the earlier Book know that this is sent down from your Lord in truth.
Answers a denial of messengership by citing God and whoever has knowledge of the Scripture.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you hold true rests on somebody having testified to it: a teacher, a parent, a book you trust. That is not a weakness in your faith; it is how nearly all human knowledge travels. Today, when someone tells you something, register consciously that you are receiving testimony, and ask what kind of witness they are.

studies.title: The Witnesses Will Say
studies.meaning: A rhetorical question ranks one offence above every other, and then the scene changes into a courtroom. The accused are brought forward and displayed, and the verdict is not pronounced by the judge but spoken aloud by witnesses. Commentators differ over who these witnesses are, naming angels, prophets, and a person's own limbs, and they set the readings out side by side. The closing word means being placed at a distance rather than being sworn at.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following a passage about people whose whole aim terminates in this world. The charge of inventing things about God ran in both directions in Mecca: the leadership levelled it at the message, and this surah answered that a few ayat earlier with the challenge to produce ten chapters. Here the same charge is turned back on the accusers.

keyTerms.note: The verb of cutting and stitching, used of manufacturing a claim. The same word was aimed at the Quran a few ayat earlier, so the surah is returning an accusation rather than raising a fresh one.
Used of troops paraded for inspection and of goods laid out for a buyer. It implies being brought forward to be looked at, rather than merely being summoned to answer for something.
A plural of the word for one who testifies. Commentators identify them variously as angels, as prophets, or as a person's own limbs, and present the readings without choosing between them.
The noun means distancing. It is not an imprecation but the state of being put far from mercy, which is why the ayah names it as a condition rather than as something spoken.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal assembly settled disputes in the open. The parties stood where everyone could see them, witnesses were called by name, and being seen to be wrong often weighed more than whatever penalty followed. Formal expulsion, the cutting of a man from his tribe's protection, left him with no water rights and nobody obliged to avenge him. Both halves of this scene were familiar.
studies.didYouKnow: The question that opens this ayah, asking who does greater wrong, is used nine times in the Quran, always as a heading placed before one specific offence: obstructing places of worship, concealing testimony, turning from a reminder, and here inventing lies about God. The grammatical shape is identical each time, and no answer is ever supplied.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Lying about God is ranked above other wrongs because it corrupts the source rather than the conduct. Everything a person does downstream of a false picture of God is built on that picture, which is why invention is treated as graver than disobedience. Having the verdict spoken by witnesses rather than by God adds something further: the judgement is not only imposed, it is recognised and said aloud by those who saw.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same opening question of the same two offences, fabricating against God and denying His signs.
Puts the identical question over a different offence, turning away from a reminder already received.
Names the witnesses concretely: tongues, hands and feet testifying about what a person did.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the sentence beginning God wants in your own speech this week, and each time you catch it, ask whether you actually know that or are extending a guess. Most of us hold small opinions about God we have never checked. Saying that you do not know about one of them today is not a loss of faith. It is accuracy.

studies.title: Seeking To Bend The Road
studies.meaning: The wrongdoers of the previous ayah get a description in three parts: they block the road, they want it bent, and they reject what stands at its end. Then their situation is stated flatly. There is nowhere on earth far enough to be out of reach, and no ally outside God to appeal to. The strangest clause comes last, that they were unable to hear and unable to see, which commentators read as an incapacity grown out of refusal rather than one they were born with.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Obstruction was a practical matter in that city rather than a figure of speech. Pilgrims arriving for the season were warned off in advance, followers of the message were pressured through their own families, and anyone without a protecting clan was the most exposed of all. The surah is describing a policy its first listeners could have named.

keyTerms.note: The verb is transitive, so the fault named is not their own refusal but their work on other people. It covers both blocking a road and diverting somebody already walking along it.
Used of a bend in something that ought to be straight, including a defect of character. Wanting a road crooked means wanting the way itself altered, not merely stepping off it.
From a root meaning to render incapable. It describes someone who gets far enough away that a pursuer is defeated, and the ayah denies that any such position exists on earth.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca controlled the roads. Its standing rested on guaranteeing safe passage to the sanctuary, and the same families who profited from pilgrim traffic could quietly steer arrivals away from a man they wanted ignored. The desert, meanwhile, offered genuine escape to anyone who could reach it, since a fugitive who found another tribe's protection was usually beyond recovery.
studies.didYouKnow: The doubling of punishment named here is explained elsewhere in the Quran as an addition rather than a multiplication: at 16:25 those who misled others carry their own full loads plus a share of the loads of the people they misguided. The arithmetic is deliberate, and it is why the doubling attaches to obstruction rather than to disbelief on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two failures that usually get collapsed together. Being wrong is one thing; working to make other people wrong is a different and heavier thing, and the doubled punishment is attached only to the second. The closing clause about hearing and sight then makes its own point, that faculties can be lost through disuse, so the condition described is an outcome rather than a starting handicap.

crossReferences.why: Adds punishment upon punishment for those who obstruct other people from the path of God.
Describes the same people in nearly identical words, hindering from the path and seeking to distort it.
Describes hearts, eyes and ears that exist and go unused, and calls that condition worse than cattle.

studies.applyIt: Consider whether anyone has ever found a good thing harder because of you: a colleague you discouraged, a sibling whose enthusiasm you flattened, a friend whose new habit you teased. You do not need to make a speech about it. Just stop doing that particular thing this week, and if it turns out to be easy, say one sentence to the person.

studies.title: The Ones Who Lost Themselves
studies.meaning: Two short ayat finish the passage in the vocabulary of trade. What these people lost is themselves, the one asset a merchant never enters in his accounts, and what they had invented has wandered off and cannot be found when it is wanted. Commentators point to the irony in that verb: the gods they made were supposed to guide, and they turn out to be the ones that go missing. A superlative closes the passage, stated with no hedging at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, ending a run of ayat that began with the person who wants only this life and is paid for it in full. The surah is speaking to a commercial city, and the closing image is drawn from it: a balance sheet on which everything came out even except the trader himself.

keyTerms.note: A merchant's word for capital sunk in a failed venture, not for something merely mislaid. Applying it to the self turns the person into the stake rather than the one holding it.
The verb usually describes a traveller losing the road. Here the invented gods do the straying, so whatever was supposed to guide becomes the thing that cannot be located.
A superlative from the trading root, so the ayah ranks them rather than simply condemning them. In a city of merchants this was the strongest available way to end an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan trader lived by his accounts. Capital was assembled from several partners, sent north with an agent, and settled on return, and a venture that came home short ruined reputations along with balances. Everyone listening had watched someone lose everything on a single caravan. Being told a man could settle every account and still be the biggest loser landed in familiar language.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's word for loss is commercial, and so are its images for gain: reciting, praying and spending are described at 35:29 as a trade that will not fail, and faith is offered at 61:10 as a bargain. This surah runs the same vocabulary at both ends, promising full payment for worldly aims a few ayat earlier and total loss here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the self as what was lost relocates the stakes entirely. The passage does not say these people lost paradise or lost their wealth; it says they lost themselves, which makes the hereafter a question of what someone has become rather than of what has been confiscated. The invented gods going missing is the practical form of that: what a life rests on decides whether anything is there at the end.

crossReferences.why: Defines the real losers in the same terms, as those who lose their own souls and their families.
Says what is invoked besides God is heedless, and becomes hostile to its worshippers when all are gathered.
Shows the same discovery arriving too late, when what they invoked has vanished from them.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of the things your life is actually resting on right now. Not what you value in principle: what you organise your weeks around. Then, beside each one, write how long you expect it to be there. The exercise takes five minutes and it is unusually clarifying, especially about the items you hesitate over.

studies.title: Those Who Became Still
studies.meaning: After a long description of loss, the counterpart arrives in a single ayah with three conditions. Belief and good deeds are the familiar pair; the third verb is rare and is what this ayah adds. It describes a settling, a becoming quiet before God, and commentators gloss it as resistance leaving a person rather than as anything performed. The reward is then stated as belonging, they are the Garden's own people, before being made permanent.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed as the direct answer to the passage on those who lost themselves. The believers being addressed were mostly without power in Mecca, so an ayah promising them permanence rather than reversal answered their actual situation. They were not being told they would win the argument, only that there was somewhere they belonged.

keyTerms.note: The root describes low, level ground that gives easily underfoot. Applied to a person it means the resistance has gone out of them, so what is named is a settling rather than an act carried out.
The first word means those who habitually accompany something, close associates rather than visitors. It makes the Garden a belonging rather than a place they are granted entry to.
The root suggests something that stays and does not decay. Arabic used it of long-lasting things generally, and the Quran fixes it to permanence beyond any measured term at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ground mattered in Arabia. Travellers looked for level, yielding land to pitch on, because a camp on hard or broken ground meant a bad night and a slow start the next morning. The word this ayah uses for humility comes from exactly that kind of ground, low and soft and easy to settle onto. The image would have arrived before the concept did.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as humbled themselves occurs only once in the entire Quran, in this ayah. Two related forms appear in the twenty-second surah, describing the same disposition, and that is the whole of the root's Quranic use. In a chapter of a hundred and twenty-three ayat it is among the rarest words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three things are required and only one of them can be seen. Belief and deeds are both observable in some form; the third is not, and it is what this ayah adds to an otherwise familiar formula. Classical commentators read it as the difference between compliance and consent. Naming the reward as companionship then matches the condition, since those who stopped resisting are described as already belonging.

crossReferences.why: Uses the related word and describes them: hearts that tremble at God's mention, patient under what strikes them.
Describes the servants of the Merciful walking the earth in humility, answering the ignorant with peace.
Pairs belief and good deeds with the identical promise, companions of the Garden abiding forever.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you argue with God without noticing that you are doing it. It usually sounds like a running commentary on why some particular circumstance ought to have gone differently. Today, when that commentary starts up, let one round of it go unspoken and unfinished. You do not have to approve of the circumstance. This ayah is asking for something quieter than approval.

studies.title: The Blind And The Seeing
studies.meaning: The comparison is built out of four terms rather than two, and commentators note that it can be read in two ways: either each party carries two descriptions, or one is blind and deaf while the other sees and hears. The question that follows is not really a question. What it does is shift the argument from theology onto ordinary judgement, since nobody supposes that a sighted man and a blind one are in the same position on a journey.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's opening section just before the prophet narratives begin. The two parties are the ones described in the preceding ayat: people whose aims end in this world, and people who believed and grew still. The parable sits exactly where argument gives way to history, so it works as a summary rather than as a fresh claim.

keyTerms.note: The word covers a comparison, a proverb and a constructed example. The Quran uses it to move an argument onto ground where a listener's own judgement can work, which is what the following question relies on.
A dual form, so the ayah counts exactly two and no more. The root concerns splitting, which makes the parties pieces of something divided rather than two competing opinions.
The verb is about remembering rather than reasoning something out afresh. It implies the comparison is not new information but something the listener already knows and has failed to apply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness was common and consequential in Arabia. Sand, sun and untreated infection took the sight of many, and a blind man in a caravan society could not travel, trade or fight; he depended entirely on kin. Deafness cut a person out of the poetry, the negotiation and the news a settlement ran on. To that audience these were not figures of speech but neighbours.
studies.didYouKnow: This particular phrase for the two parties appears three times in the Quran, and each time inside a dispute about which side is better placed. Here the answer is left with the listener. At 19:73 the disbelievers ask the same question about themselves and settle it by pointing at their own furnishings and gatherings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parable makes disbelief a matter of capacity rather than of conclusion. What is being compared is not two arguments but two conditions, one able to receive and one not, which is why the passage ends by asking for reflection instead of producing more evidence. It also keeps the faculties ordinary: seeing and hearing, not some additional sense granted to a few.

crossReferences.why: Ends a list of denials with the same question in shorter form, are the blind and the seeing alike.
Extends the comparison through darkness and light, shade and heat, and finally the living and the dead.
Locates the blindness precisely: it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts inside the chests.

studies.applyIt: Pick one subject you have decided you already understand: a person, an old disagreement, a criticism somebody gave you. Spend ten minutes today taking in new information about it without forming any view. Read, or listen, and stop there. The ayah is about capacity, and capacity is trained by using it on something you had closed.

studies.title: The Oldest Message There Is
studies.meaning: The first narrative opens with almost the words the surah itself opened with. Noah says he is a plain warner and states one thing, to worship none but God, which is exactly what the surah's second ayah said. Commentators note the echo as deliberate: the message being refused in Mecca is shown to be the oldest message there is. What Noah adds is the word fear, and he uses it about them rather than at them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The narratives in this surah are addressed to a community under sustained pressure, and their purpose is stated later in the chapter, to steady the heart of the one receiving them. Noah comes first because his mission ran longest and gathered fewest, which makes him the most useful precedent for a small group in a hostile city.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means both clear in itself and making other things clear. It forecloses the charge of ambiguity, since a warner described this way leaves his hearers no room to say they misunderstood.

The root is that of a servant bound to a master, so worship in this vocabulary is service and belonging before it is ritual feeling. The negative construction makes exclusivity the entire content of the demand.
The preposition aims the fear towards them rather than at them. It is the construction used of someone anxious about another person's safety, which makes this warning an expression of concern.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan audience knew Noah as a name from the older stories that travelled the trade routes, told by Jewish and Christian communities in Yathrib, in Najran, and along the road to Syria. What this surah supplies is not the flood, which they had heard about, but the arguing before it: the conversations between one man and his people over many years.
studies.didYouKnow: Noah's demand here is worded almost identically to the surah's own second ayah, that you worship none but God. The same demand, in a slightly different formula, then opens the speech of Hud to Aad, of Salih to Thamud, and of Shuaib to Median later in the chapter. One message is delivered five times in a hundred and twenty-three ayat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting Noah's words in the same shape as the surah's opening makes a claim about revelation itself: it is not developing over time, it is recurring. That has a consequence for how rejection should be read, since the objections raised against Noah in the following ayat are the objections Mecca was raising. The passage also sets warning inside concern, which keeps the threat from being merely punitive.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah named after Noah with the same commission: warn them, worship God, and be mindful.
Gives Noah's opening words in nearly the same form, including the fear of a tremendous Day.
States the rule these narratives illustrate: every messenger was sent with this single message.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you believe you first heard from someone who was worried about you. Warnings from people who love us rarely arrive as information; they arrive as anxiety, and we register the tone and lose the content. Think of one you dismissed for that reason, and consider its content today on its own.

studies.title: Only Our Lowest Followed You
studies.meaning: Three objections are raised and every one of them is about status. He is only a man like us; the people following him are our lowest, and they joined without thinking; he has nothing that puts him above us. Commentators observe that not one objection touches anything Noah actually said. The verb see is repeated three times, and then even that is downgraded in the last clause, where seeing becomes merely thinking.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the parallel to the surah's own moment is not subtle. The early followers in Mecca included a large proportion of slaves, freed men and the young, and the recorded objection from the city's leadership was the same one: that men of standing could not be expected to sit beside such people. The same complaint is attributed to Noah's chiefs across several surahs.

keyTerms.note: A word for the men who fill a space and dominate it, used throughout the Quran for the leadership of a people. It names them by their weight in a gathering rather than by any office they held.
A word for the worn out or discarded, applied to goods before people. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it reveals more about the speakers' scale of value than about anyone it describes.
The phrase means a judgement formed on the surface without looking further. The chiefs use it to dismiss the followers' conviction as hasty, which is itself a judgement made at a glance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in an Arabian town was not an opinion but an arrangement. Where a man sat in the assembly, whether his testimony was accepted, whether his daughter could marry into a particular house, all followed from lineage and wealth. A movement drawing its numbers from the bottom of that arrangement did not look like a threat to belief. It looked like a threat to the seating.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Noah's chiefs use for his followers, meaning our most worthless, occurs only once in the whole Quran. A related form appears once more at 26:111, where the same objection is put to the same prophet in almost the same words. It is as close as the Quran comes to repeating one specific insult.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records an argument that is entirely social and lets it stand on its own terms, because Noah's reply in the ayat that follow refuses the frame rather than disputing the facts. What it establishes is that objections to revelation are often objections to its company. The chiefs never claim the message is false; they claim the people carrying it are beneath them.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same objection to Noah and receives the same refusal to send the believers away.
Records identical pressure on the Prophet, with the instruction not to drive the poor from his company.
Shows the demand that revelation should have come to a great man from one of the two cities.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group whose views you dismiss partly because of who holds them. Not people who are wrong, but people you would find it embarrassing to agree with. Read one thing this week by someone inside that group and judge it on what it says. This is harder than it sounds, and the difficulty is precisely the point of the ayah.

studies.title: Can We Force It On You
studies.meaning: The reply does not engage with the insults at all. It offers a supposition, and then asks a question about method: suppose the evidence is real and you cannot see it, am I then supposed to fasten it onto you? Commentators dwell on the final clause, that they dislike it, which acknowledges the resistance instead of treating it as mere ignorance. The mercy Noah mentions is understood as prophethood itself, given to him rather than earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and read by commentators as consolation and instruction together. The community around the Prophet had no power to compel anybody, and this passage turns that into a principle rather than a limitation. The formula rendered have you considered opens three separate speeches in this surah, appearing in the mouths of Noah, Salih and Shuaib alike.

keyTerms.note: Literally have you seen, used to open a supposition. It invites the listener into a scenario rather than asserting it, which is why the whole reply takes the form of a question rather than a counter-claim.

Commentators read this of prophethood and the revelation that comes with it. Calling it mercy rather than authority makes it something received, which the chiefs' complaint about rank cannot account for.

keyTerms.gloss: shall we fasten it on you
keyTerms.note: The verb means making something stick to a person, the way a debt or a duty attaches. The form piles two pronouns onto it, which gives the question its slightly incredulous weight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Compulsion was how most things moved in that world. A chief's decision bound his clan, a father's word settled a marriage, and a defeated tribe adopted the religion of its conqueror as a matter of course. Against that background, a man claiming divine backing and then asking whether he could possibly force it on anyone was saying something structurally strange.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening formula here, have you considered, is placed in the mouths of three different prophets within this one surah: Noah in this ayah, Salih to Thamud at 11:63, and Shuaib to Median at 11:88. Each time it introduces the same hypothetical, that the speaker really does stand on clear evidence from his Lord.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once. Guidance is described as something given, which removes it from the economy of status the chiefs were arguing inside, and compulsion is ruled out in the strongest form available, a rhetorical question expecting the answer no. Notably this is done while assuming the speaker is right. The refusal to compel is not doubt about the truth; it sits alongside certainty.

crossReferences.why: States as a principle what this ayah puts as a question: there is no compulsion in religion.
Asks whether you would compel people to believe, when God did not will everyone on earth to.
Tells the Prophet he is no dictator over them, and to remind by the Quran whoever fears the warning.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have been trying to convince of something you are sure about. Notice how much of your effort goes into pressure, the repetition, the timing, a certain tone, rather than into the case itself. Try one conversation this week where you say the thing once, clearly, and then stop. Watch what you feel in the moment you stop.

studies.title: I Will Not Drive Them Away
studies.meaning: Two things are refused in a single breath: payment, and the removal of the poor believers. The second refusal is the substantial one, since the chiefs had made it the price of their attention. Noah's reason is not that the believers deserve better but that they are going to meet their Lord, which puts the decision outside his authority. Then he asks who would defend him if he did it, turning the chiefs' protection into the thing actually at risk.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Reports from this period describe leading Meccans proposing that the Prophet hold separate sessions, or send the poorer followers away, before they would consent to listen. Commentators connect this passage and its parallels to that pressure, while treating the Noah narrative as history in its own right rather than as an allegory of the Meccan situation.

keyTerms.note: The word covers wealth of any kind, and especially livestock, which was its commonest form. Refusing it establishes that nothing in the message is transactional before anything else gets argued.
The verb is used of chasing off animals and of expelling a person from a gathering. Naming himself as not that sort of man makes the refusal a matter of character rather than of policy.
The root covers both not knowing and acting rashly, and pre-Islamic Arabia used it for a whole temper of impulsive, prideful conduct. The charge concerns behaviour, not the absence of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poets and orators were paid. A skilled tongue could be hired to praise a tribe or to destroy a rival's name, and the going rates were common knowledge, so a man who spoke publicly and refused money was making a claim about himself that his audience would test. The membership of a gathering was equally serious, since who sat in it decided who else would come.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase Noah uses for refusing to drive the believers away occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 26:114, both times in his mouth. The same instruction is later given directly to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at 6:52, telling him not to send away those who call on their Lord morning and evening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds equality in accountability rather than in sentiment. The believers cannot be driven off because they are going to meet their Lord, which makes their standing a matter of what God will do rather than of what anybody currently thinks of them. Refusing payment does related work, removing the one motive that would have made the message negotiable.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the Prophet in the same terms not to drive away those who call on their Lord.
Tells him to stay content with them and not let his eyes pass beyond them towards worldly glitter.
Names the mark of a true guide: he asks you for no wage and is himself already guided.

studies.applyIt: Consider who you would be a little embarrassed to be seen with. Not people you dislike, but people whose company might cost you something socially. If someone in that description has a claim on your time this week, a call, an invitation, a favour, take it, and do not quietly arrange for it to happen in private.

studies.title: Four Things I Do Not Claim
studies.meaning: Four denials arrive in a row and they run in a particular direction. Noah gives up wealth, hidden knowledge, and any claim to be more than human. Then he refuses a fourth thing nobody had asked him to claim: the right to pronounce on the inner state of the people his opponents despise. That is the one he attaches a penalty to. Commentators observe that the passage defines prophethood almost entirely by what it does not include.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demands recorded earlier in this surah were precisely for a treasure and an angel, which the twelfth ayah names, so the answer given to Noah's chiefs also answers Mecca's own conditions. The commentators read the passage as clearing away a set of expectations about what a messenger must be before the narrative is allowed to continue.

keyTerms.note: The word is used of a treasury or a granary, a place where reserves are kept against need. Denying possession of them separates the messenger's role from any power over how provision is distributed.
Whatever is absent from perception, hidden in the present or still to come. Denying knowledge of it puts a prophet in exactly the same position as everybody else with regard to tomorrow.
The verb means to reckon something of little worth, and attaching it to eyes locates the contempt in a look. It is reported as the chiefs' valuation, and the ayah declines to adopt it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A granary was where a settlement's survival was stored. Whoever held its keys held the town through a bad year, and the position was watched closely and resented easily. Claiming the storehouses of God would have been the largest claim a man could make in that world, which is why Noah's denial of it comes first, immediately after he has refused money.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three-part disclaimer, the storehouses of God, knowledge of the unseen, and being an angel, appears almost word for word in another surah, where it is spoken by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) instead of by Noah. The two passages are close enough that classical commentators habitually treat them together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophethood is defined here by subtraction. What remains after the denials is a man carrying a message, which is exactly the thing the chiefs had said was not enough. The fourth denial reaches further than the other three: refusing to pronounce on what God will give people whose insides he cannot see makes humility a question of jurisdiction, and calling the opposite wrongdoing places it in this surah's gravest category.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical three denials in the Prophet's mouth, closing with the blind and the seeing.
Denies him control over benefit or harm and any knowledge of the unseen, with the same reasoning.
Warns against declaring your own purity, since He knows best who has been mindful of Him.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you decide, silently, that someone is not going to change. That verdict usually arrives fully formed and feels like realism. Noah refuses to make it even about people who are insulting him. Today, hold one such conclusion loosely for an hour, and notice how much of your behaviour towards that person it had quietly been organising.

studies.title: Bring It On Us Then
studies.meaning: The debate collapses. The chiefs do not answer the argument; they complain about its length and demand the punishment instead, which is a way of ending a conversation by daring the other side to finish it. Noah's reply corrects the ownership of the threat. He is not the one who brings it, God is, and its arrival is conditional on will rather than on anything Noah says. The final clause closes an exit they had not thought to ask about.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demand it records was being made in Mecca at the same time. Commentators note where it falls inside Noah's mission: the argument had already run a very long time by this point, and the request to have done with it comes out of exhaustion as much as out of defiance.

keyTerms.note: The root is used of twisting a rope tight. Argument in this word is a contest of holds rather than an exchange of reasons, which suits a complaint about how long the contest has gone on.
A condition attached to the very punishment they demanded. It takes the timing out of the messenger's hands, so their challenge cannot be settled by anything he says or fails to produce.
The word describes someone who has put himself past a pursuer's power. Denying it answers the practical question underneath the taunt, which is whether the threat could be outrun.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian disputes were often settled by a public wager or a dare, and both sides understood the form: name your terms, produce your proof, or withdraw. Demanding that a man make good on his threat was a recognised way of winding up an argument you had tired of, and the audience would expect the challenged party either to deliver or to lose standing.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah uses the verb for disputing twice, at opposite ends of the same chapter and about opposite things. Here the chiefs accuse Noah of arguing with them far too much. Later, at 11:74, Abraham is described as arguing with God on behalf of the people of Lot. The word carries no judgement of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply separates the messenger from the outcome twice over. God brings it, and He brings it if He wills, so a delay proves nothing about the warning and an arrival would prove nothing about the warner's power. That is a consistent position across this surah, which has already told the Prophet that his work is warning and that the rest is entrusted elsewhere.

crossReferences.why: Records the same demand made to Lot: bring us God's punishment, if you are one of the truthful.
Preserves a Meccan version of it, asking for stones from the sky or a painful affliction.
Answers the demand for haste by saying the decision rests with God, not with the messenger.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you end a disagreement by daring the other person rather than by answering them. It sounds like go on then, prove it, and it feels a little like winning. The next time you hear that in your own voice, treat it as a signal that you have run out of argument, and say so instead. It is a more honest place to stop.

studies.title: The Limit Of Good Advice
studies.meaning: Noah states the boundary of his own work. Sincere counsel, offered with full intent, does not produce its effect by itself; if God wills that a people be left to their error, the advice passes straight through them. Commentators are careful at this point, reading the abandonment described as a consequence of persistent refusal rather than an arbitrary decision, and linking it to the many places where turning away comes first and being turned away follows after.
