studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the close of Noah's long argument with his people and immediately before the revelation that none of the rest will believe. Placed there, the ayah prepares the ending. Commentators read it as the moment a very long mission is honestly appraised from the inside, by the man who has been conducting it.

keyTerms.note: The root carries purity, used of honey free of wax, and also of stitching a tear closed. Advice in this word is unmixed with self-interest and aimed at repairing the person it is offered to.
A verb of disappointment and error. Commentators read it as God leaving people to the direction they have already chosen, and connect it to the ayat where refusal precedes abandonment.
A passive, so the returning is not something they undertake. Ending the sentence there places the whole disagreement inside a movement already under way, whichever side of it a person is standing on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Advice had a formal place in Arabian life. A man of standing was expected to counsel his kin, and refusing counsel from someone with a duty to give it was a recognised breach. The word used here also carried the sense of loyal service owed to a chief. Noah is speaking the vocabulary of a relationship they still had, at the exact point where it stops working.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sincere counsel in this ayah shares its root with the word for sewing. Arabic lexicographers connect the two senses through the idea of closing a gap: honey purified of its wax, a tear stitched shut, and advice given with nothing foreign mixed into it. The same root gives the ordinary word for a tailor.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts the outcome of guidance outside the guide, which protects a sincere person from measuring himself by results. It also refuses the opposite error, since Noah neither stops advising nor concludes that effort is pointless; he keeps offering counsel while admitting it may not land. Both halves matter, and the surah holds them together without resolving the tension between them.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit directly to the Prophet: you cannot guide whom you love, but God guides.
Says their guidance is not your responsibility, immediately before speaking about giving to them anyway.
Asks whether you would compel people, then says no soul believes except by God's leave.

studies.applyIt: If you have been advising someone for a long time with no effect, try changing what you measure. Instead of asking whether they have moved, ask whether your last three attempts were actually for them or partly for you. Then decide whether to say it once more or to leave it for now. This ayah permits both.

studies.title: Upon Me Falls My Crime
studies.meaning: The narrative stops and the surah turns to address its own audience. The accusation is the one raised twenty ayat earlier, in exactly the same three words, but the answer this time is different. Instead of a challenge, it offers a division of liability: if the charge is true, the guilt is mine and stays with me, while whatever you are doing remains yours. Commentators note that the reply concedes nothing at all while declining to argue.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators generally treat this ayah as a parenthesis: the story of Noah pauses and the address turns to the Prophet and his opponents before the narrative resumes in the following ayah. Others read it as still inside the story, spoken by Noah to his own people, and the classical sources record both readings side by side.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used against the Quran at the thirteenth ayah of this surah, in the identical three-word opening. The repetition marks a deliberate return to an accusation the chapter has already answered once.
The root is used of cutting fruit from a tree, and came to mean severing yourself from what is right. The possessive makes the liability personal, which is the entire structure of the reply.
The word means free of a debt or healed of a disease. It describes a separation that is already complete rather than one being argued for, which is why no further defence follows it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Liability in Arabia was collective by default. A killing by one man could be answered on any member of his clan, and a debt could follow a family for a generation, which made untangling who owed what a constant public business. Someone offering to carry his own consequences alone was refusing the ordinary arrangement everyone around him lived under.
studies.didYouKnow: The three-word phrase that opens this ayah, asking whether they say he made it up, occurs seven times in the Quran and twice inside this single surah: at 11:13, where it is met with the challenge to produce ten chapters, and here, where it is met instead with an offer to divide the blame between the parties.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The response separates the question of truth from the question of consequence, which is an unusual move. It does not assert that the accusation is false; it says that even on the accusers' own account the liability is his alone and does not reach them, while theirs stays with them. That framing makes each person's answer their own, a position the Quran takes repeatedly about the last day.

crossReferences.why: Divides responsibility in the same way when he is accused of lying: my deeds mine, yours yours.
Says neither party will be questioned about the other's deeds, and leaves the judging to God.
Ends a refusal with the same clean division: you have your way and I have mine.

studies.applyIt: When you are accused of something you did not do, the instinct is to argue the facts, then the tone, then the accuser's motives. Try answering once, plainly, and then leaving the question of who is right exactly where it lies. Notice how much energy you would normally spend past that point, and where it actually goes.

studies.title: Do Not Grieve Over Them
studies.meaning: A mission is closed by revelation rather than by a decision. Noah is told the list is complete and that nobody further will believe. What follows is not an instruction to stop working but an instruction about feeling, do not take their conduct into yourself, which commentators take as the real point of the ayah. The grief in question is a prophet's grief over people, and it is being released rather than reproached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the commentators note the length of what has just ended. Another surah gives Noah's stay among his people as nine hundred and fifty years, so the verdict delivered here closes an effort on a scale attributed to no other prophet. The ayah itself says nothing about that. It addresses only what he is to feel from this point on.

keyTerms.note: The passive keeps the messenger out of the judgement: Noah does not conclude this, he is told it. The root suggests something conveyed quickly and privately, which is how prophetic communication is generally described.

An emphatic future negation, closing a possibility rather than reporting a present state. Commentators read it as a verdict on people whose refusal had settled, not as a statement about human nature at large.
The verb is reflexive, naming the act of taking misery into yourself. It addresses the inward absorption of grief rather than sorrow itself, which is what makes such an instruction possible at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long labour with nothing to show for it was familiar in that world. A well could be dug through rock for months and come up dry, a herd bred carefully over years could be lost in one bad season, and a man might spend a lifetime pressing a claim his sons would still be pursuing. That audience understood work whose result lay outside the worker's hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for Noah's distress appears in this form only twice in the whole Quran, and both times as an instruction not to feel it. The other occurrence is at 12:69, where Joseph tells his youngest brother not to be saddened by what the others had been doing to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes a careful separation. The outcome of a mission is settled elsewhere, and the messenger's attachment to that outcome is treated as a distinct matter requiring its own instruction. That God gives the instruction at all takes the grief seriously; it is neither denied nor reasoned away. Noah is simply told that he may now put it down.

crossReferences.why: Gives the Prophet the same two instructions together: do not grieve over them, do not be distressed.
Names the risk exactly, that he might destroy himself with grief chasing after their belief.
Records Noah's own prayer at the very end, and which people he asks to be covered instead.

studies.applyIt: There is probably one person whose choices you carry as though they were partly yours to fix. You may not be able to change what you want for them. You can sometimes change how much of your day their situation occupies. Pick one hour today and deliberately do not think about it; when it comes back, notice it and set it down again.

studies.title: Build It Under Our Eyes
studies.meaning: The instruction is practical and the reassurance is folded into it. Build, and do it under Our eyes and by Our instruction, so the work is supervised at every point. Then comes a harder prohibition: do not speak to Me about the wrongdoers. Commentators read this as closing the door on intercession for a group whose case is already settled, and they note that it arrives before the flood rather than after, so Noah knows in advance what he may not ask.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The building of the vessel occupies several ayat here and almost none in the parallel accounts, which the commentators connect to what this surah is for. A community waiting for relief in Mecca is shown a prophet given a long, visible, ridiculed task to carry out during the interval between a verdict and its execution.

keyTerms.note: In Arabic usage this is a phrase of protection rather than surveillance, close to saying under our care. The Quran uses it four times, always of something done openly and under God's keeping.
The same word used for revelation given to prophets, applied here to the practical design of a vessel. It makes the shipbuilding a form of guidance rather than an errand carried out afterwards.
The verb is of speaking to someone directly and face to face. The prohibition concerns raising the subject at all, which is considerably stronger than a refusal of the request would have been.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There was no shipbuilding tradition in inland Arabia. Mecca knew vessels from the Red Sea ports and from traders who had crossed to Abyssinia, but its own carpentry served houses, saddles and wells. A man constructing something enormous far from any water would have looked to that audience precisely as the next ayah reports he looked to his own people.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase under Our eyes occurs four times in the Quran, and three of them belong to this one event: the building of the vessel here, its building again at 23:27, and its sailing at 54:14. The fourth is an instruction to the Prophet at 52:48 to wait patiently for his Lord's decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Supervision and prohibition arrive in the same sentence, and both are forms of nearness. Being watched over is offered as reassurance during a task with no visible sense to it, while the ban on pleading marks a limit that even a prophet's closeness does not cross. Placing the verdict before the event also means the flood carries out a judgement rather than constituting one.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in nearly identical words, with the same prohibition attached to it.
Describes the vessel itself, planks and nails, sailing before Our eyes, and left behind as a sign.
Applies the same phrase to the Prophet: wait for your Lord's decision, you are before Our eyes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are doing that will not make sense to anyone for a long time: a course you are studying, a habit you are rebuilding, a relationship you are repairing slowly. Do the next piece of it today without explaining it to anybody. The reassurance in this ayah is not that the work will be understood. It is that it is seen.

studies.title: Whenever They Passed By Him
studies.meaning: The scene is drawn in a continuous tense, so it repeats: they keep passing, they keep laughing. Noah's answer is unusual and the commentators handle it with care. He does not dispute the absurdity of what he is doing; he says the laughter will change direction, and he uses their own verb to say it. What follows names two punishments rather than one, a disgrace that arrives soon and something lasting that does not leave.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a city where ridicule was the main instrument used against the message. Mockery cost nothing, required no argument, and worked on the followers rather than on the leader. This surah gives more room to the ark's construction than to the flood, which the commentators connect to the period of exposure a community has to live through before anything changes.

keyTerms.note: A continuous tense, so the ayah pictures the work still under way as they pass. The verb belongs to craft and manufacture, the ordinary word for a tradesman at his bench rather than a builder of marvels.

The root is that of putting something at your own disposal. Mockery in this word subordinates the other person, which is why the reply speaks about the direction of the mockery rather than about hurt feelings.
From a root meaning shame and exposure. It names the first punishment by its social effect, which is an exact answer to a mockery whose whole purpose had been to shame.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A workshop in an Arabian town stood open to the street. Carpenters, smiths and tanners worked where passers-by could watch and comment, and a craftsman's reputation was made or lost in that traffic. Noah building something enormous and unexplained in full view, day after day for years, was not a private eccentricity. It was a public performance he could not stop.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions the vessel in more than twenty places, but the sustained scene of construction, of people passing and laughing, and of the reply given to them belongs to this surah alone. The chapter later states its own purpose in exactly those terms, as material meant to steady the heart of the one receiving it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes that mockery is answered by outcome rather than by argument. Noah does not defend the project or explain where water would come from; he says only that the positions will reverse and that both sides will find out which way. Naming two punishments, one that shames and one that lasts, separates the social sting from the real consequence, so the answer is not merely an insult returned.

crossReferences.why: States the pattern plainly: no messenger ever came to them without being ridiculed for it.
Reverses the same scene at the end, with the believers on couches looking at what became of the mockers.
Says messengers before were ridiculed, and what they jeered at closed in around the jeerers.

studies.applyIt: Being laughed at is a specific kind of pressure, and it works on people who are otherwise brave. If you are doing something ordinary and good that somebody in your life finds funny, do not defend it and do not stop it. Just carry on with the next piece of it today. Noah's answer was not a comeback. It was that he kept building.

studies.title: When The Oven Boiled Over
studies.meaning: The signal is domestic and strange: an oven boils over. Commentators offer several readings, that water rose from the household ovens, that the word names a particular place, or that it describes the surface of the earth breaking open, and they set the range out without deciding. What follows is an inventory rather than a scene. Pairs of every kind, the household with one exception already announced, and the believers, counted last and described as few.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators discuss the exception clause closely, since it announces the loss of a family member before the reader has met him. That is a narrative choice with a purpose: the passage soon after, in which Noah appeals for his son, is read against a verdict the reader already knows had been given in advance.

keyTerms.note: A domestic clay oven sunk into the ground. Commentators differ over whether the word is literal here, names a particular place, or stands for the earth's surface, and they record the readings without choosing.
The doubling is emphatic. The first word already means one of a pair, so adding two makes the instruction unmistakable about numbers, which mattered for a cargo expected to reproduce afterwards.
The clause ends the ayah on a count. After the pairs and the household, the believers turn out to be the smallest item on the manifest, and that is the detail the surah leaves with its first readers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The clay oven was the centre of a household. It was where the day's bread was made, often shared between neighbouring families, and it sat low in the ground where a woman would kneel to work at it. Choosing that object as the sign that the flood had started located the end of a world at the most domestic point in the house.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to load two of every pair occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 23:27, and the same phrase turns up once more at 13:3, where it describes the two kinds God placed in every fruit. The oven boiling over is likewise mentioned only in this ayah and its counterpart in the twenty-third surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah pairs the preservation of every kind with the smallness of the believing group and simply lets the contrast stand. Continuity of creation is guaranteed while the community that recognised God is described as a handful, which sets numbers aside as a measure of anything. The exception clause does further work: mercy in this passage operates by name rather than by household or category.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same command in nearly identical terms, including both the oven and the pairs.
Describes the water arriving from two directions at once, gates of the sky and springs of the earth.
Recalls the same moment and says the whole event was made into a lesson for retaining ears.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the sign here was a kitchen. Whatever is coming in your life will most likely announce itself through something entirely ordinary, and you will probably not recognise it at the time. That is not an argument for hunting signs. It is an argument for treating the ordinary parts of today as though they might be carrying something.

studies.title: Its Sailing And Its Mooring
studies.meaning: The boarding is marked by a sentence rather than a ceremony. The vessel's going and its stopping are both placed in the name of God, which covers the whole voyage including the part nobody can plan for. Commentators observe that a ship's mooring mattered as much as its sailing to anyone who actually used one. Two names close the ayah, and both concern mercy rather than power, which is a striking choice at the moment a flood begins.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The formula spoken here was already familiar to the surah's first hearers in another form, since the same words open every chapter of the Quran but one. Commentators treat this ayah and its counterpart in the story of Solomon as the only two places where the phrase stands inside the text rather than at the head of a chapter.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of getting onto an animal, which was the only kind of riding most of the audience knew. Applied to a vessel it makes boarding an act of trusting yourself to something that carries you.
The noun names the motion of the vessel while it is under way. Pairing it with its opposite covers the whole voyage, since a ship in trouble is very often one that cannot stop where it needs to.
From a root meaning to be firmly fixed, the same root that gives the word for mountains set into the earth. It names the stopping as an achievement rather than as the mere absence of motion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Red Sea shipping was a known risk along the routes Meccans traded on. Vessels were sewn rather than nailed, coastal winds were unpredictable, and the dangerous part of a voyage was frequently the arrival, since a boat could survive open water and break apart trying to land. Naming both the sailing and the mooring named both halves of the danger.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase in the name of God occurs inside the body of the Quran only twice. Once here, spoken by Noah as the vessel is boarded, and once at 27:30, where it opens the letter Solomon sends to the queen of Sheba. Everywhere else in the Book the words stand at the head of a chapter rather than within an ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two names of God are chosen at the point where a judgement is being executed, and neither of them is a name of power. Commentators read the pairing as directed at those on board rather than at those outside, since the people being saved are not told they earned it. The ayah also places a formula in a prophet's mouth at the start of a journey, which is how the Quran often marks a change of state.

crossReferences.why: The only other place this phrase stands inside an ayah, opening the letter Solomon sends.
Gives a formula for mounting whatever carries you, ending on the return to your Lord.
Notes that people call on God sincerely at sea and forget the moment they reach dry land.

studies.applyIt: Notice the things you begin without marking at all: getting into a car, opening a laptop, starting a conversation you have been dreading. Pick one of them today and put a sentence at the front of it, even silently. The point is not the words. It is that you noticed a beginning while it was happening rather than afterwards.

studies.title: My Son, Embark With Us
studies.meaning: The scale of the scene and the smallness of the appeal are set side by side. Waves like mountains, and a father shouting an affectionate diminutive at his boy. Commentators notice the form of address, the one a parent uses to a small child, reached for at the last possible moment in the middle of a catastrophe. The instruction has two halves, come with us and do not stay with them, which is the choice the whole surah has been describing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The son enters the narrative here, having been announced in advance by the exception clause two ayat earlier, so the reader already knows how this ends. The classical commentators discuss how Noah himself understood that clause and record more than one view. What they agree on is that the appeal was made in complete sincerity.

keyTerms.note: The comparison occurs once in the Quran. For an audience whose landscape was defined by mountains and whose experience of water was wells and sudden torrents, it is the largest available image for water in motion.
A noun of place from a verb meaning to set aside. It describes somewhere he had put himself rather than somewhere he happened to be standing, which is how the commentators read his absence.
A diminutive with a possessive attached, the form a parent uses to a small child. Noah reaches for it at the moment of greatest danger, which makes the appeal a father's before it is a prophet's.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A son was a household's future and its security in old age, and a father's authority over one was close to absolute in Arabian custom. Sons who separated themselves from their father's household were a recognised disgrace, discussed openly and rarely mended. The first audience would have felt the weight of this scene through that lens before any theological one reached them.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison of waves to mountains occurs only here in the Quran. A related image appears at 31:32, where waves cover people like canopies and they call on God with complete sincerity until He brings them to land. Between them, these two passages are the Book's only sustained pictures of high water at sea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the strongest natural bond against belonging to the message, and does not soften the collision at all. Noah's appeal is right to make and it fails, which establishes that a prophet's sincerity does not guarantee a result even inside his own house. The two halves of his instruction also make the point that boarding and separating were one act rather than two.

crossReferences.why: Gives the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot as examples of closeness that availed them nothing.
Describes waves covering people, and the sincerity that lasts only until they are delivered to land.
Shows Abraham praying for a father, and names the point at which the asking stopped.

studies.applyIt: If there is someone in your family you have stopped inviting because the answer is always no, invite them once more this week to the smallest thing you have. Not the big conversation: a meal, a walk, a phone call at a fixed hour. Noah called out in a storm and was refused, and he still called.

studies.title: No Shelter From The Decree
studies.meaning: The son answers with a plan, and the plan is entirely reasonable. High ground is where anyone goes in a flood. The reply corrects the category rather than the geography: nothing shelters from God's command that day, and then a single exception is named, which is mercy rather than height. The final clause is short, and commentators note that the conversation is cut off mid-exchange by the water rather than brought to a conclusion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and read by commentators as the point where the surah's argument about protection is settled. The city's leadership relied on alliances, on walls, and on the standing of its sanctuary. The Noah narrative had already denied that anyone could put themselves beyond reach on the earth, and here the same denial is spoken by a father to his son.

keyTerms.note: The verb means withdrawing to a place of safety, and its noun gives the ordinary word for a dwelling. This is the plain language of finding refuge, which is exactly what makes the answer sound so sensible.
The word describes something that holds a person back from harm, like a rope that prevents a fall. The construction denies that any such thing exists that day, and this exact phrase occurs only here.
The exception names neither a place nor a means, only a recipient. Commentators read it as making mercy the sole available shelter, which is why the ayah cannot be answered by climbing any higher.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Flash floods were the deadliest ordinary danger in Arabia. Rain falling far away could send a wall of water down a dry valley within minutes, and the standing advice was precisely what the son gives here: get to high ground quickly. Mecca itself sits in a valley and was flooded more than once, so this exchange was not abstract for the first listeners.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact construction denying any protector occurs only once in the Quran, in this ayah. Its root supplies several familiar words, including the one used at 3:103 for holding fast to the rope of God. That makes the denial here quite specific: not that nothing holds a person, but that nothing does except by way of mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses a compromise readers are inclined to make, that faith and precaution are two routes to the same safety. The son takes the precaution and it fails, and the ayah offers no physical explanation of why the mountain was insufficient. Instead it relocates the category: safety was never a property of places. The exception named keeps that conclusion from becoming despair.

crossReferences.why: Describes a day of turning and fleeing with no defender against God for anyone at all.
Uses the same root positively, telling them to hold fast together to the rope of God.
Asks who delivers you from the darkness of land and sea, and answers that God alone does.

studies.applyIt: Think of the thing you rely on to keep you safe: savings, a job, a person, your own competence. None of these are wrong to have, and the ayah does not ask you to give them up. Say once today, about one of them, that it is not actually what is holding you. Then carry on using it as before.

studies.title: O Earth, Swallow Your Waters
studies.meaning: The ending is written as commands addressed to things that cannot hear. The earth is told to drink and the sky to stop, and then a sequence of short reports follows: the water went down, the matter was finished, the vessel came to rest, a verdict was announced. Commentators have long remarked on the compression. Nothing at all is described; everything is reported, and the close of a world fits into a single breath.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Judi is named here and nowhere else in the Quran. The classical commentators identify it as a mountain in the region of the upper Tigris, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, and they report that identification from the earlier traditions rather than deriving it from anything in the text itself.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of a throat taking something down, an unmistakably bodily word. Addressed to the earth it makes the ground drink, which is why translators reach for swallow rather than absorb.
Used of a person abandoning a habit, and of rain ceasing. Addressed to the sky it asks for cessation rather than for clearing, so the sequence follows the order events actually take.
A passive of a verb used of water sinking away into the ground. The passive keeps the agent out of sight, which is the pattern of every clause after the opening two commands.

A place name given only here in the whole Quran. Commentators locate it among the northern mountains and treat the identification as received from earlier tradition rather than established from the text.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia water leaving was as dramatic as water arriving. After a sudden torrent a valley floor could drink the whole of it within a day, and herdsmen judged where to graze by watching how quickly the ground took it down. Telling the earth to swallow its water described something that audience had watched, only at a scale beyond any valley they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that addresses the earth and the sky directly by name, and both of those vocatives occur nowhere else in the Book. Classical scholars of Arabic rhetoric returned to it repeatedly as an example of concentrated eloquence, since it runs from command to conclusion in a handful of words while describing nothing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The commands are given to the elements rather than to people, which places the whole event on the far side of human agency. The passive verbs then keep the actor out of view: things were said, the water was made to sink, a proclamation was made. What stays visible is the sequence rather than the power exercising it, which is a particular kind of restraint at the climax of a story.

crossReferences.why: Describes the water's arrival from two directions, which this single ayah reverses in one line.
Says the same event was made into a lesson, kept by ears able to retain what they hear.
Ends a different people with the identical closing formula, away with the wrongdoing people.

studies.applyIt: Read this ayah aloud once, slowly, in whichever translation you use, and notice how quickly it ends. Then think of something in your own life that took years and finished in an afternoon: a job, a course, an illness, a house you left. Endings are almost always shorter than we expect. Sit with that for a minute today.

studies.title: My Son Is Of My Family
studies.meaning: The prayer is built from three statements rather than a request, and commentators pay attention to that. Noah asks for nothing; he lays out what he takes to be the case. This is my household, Your promise is true, You judge best of all who judge. The request lives in the gap between the first two clauses and is never spoken. The third clause is where he stops, and it is the one that leaves room for the answer he receives.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators discuss what Noah had understood by the earlier exception, since the command to board specified his household except those already sentenced, and they record more than one view about whether he knew who was meant. What they agree on is that this prayer is offered sincerely and that it is corrected rather than condemned.

keyTerms.note: The verb is of calling across a distance, loudly enough to carry. Used for prayer twice within three ayat here, it keeps the physical situation present: a man on a boat shouting, first to a son and now upward.
The word covers family and dependants, everyone under a man's roof and his protection. It is the term the earlier promise used, which is precisely why Noah quotes it back in his prayer.
A superlative built on the root that joins judgement and wisdom. It occurs twice in the Quran, and here it works as a concession folded into the prayer before any answer has arrived.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A protected household was a legal fact in Arabia, not a sentiment. To be counted in a man's household was to be under his guarantee, entitled to his defence, and included in any agreement he entered. Noah is making a claim in exactly that language, and the answer he receives redefines who the membership covers rather than withdrawing the guarantee.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Noah ends on, wisest of all who judge, occurs twice in the Quran: here, and as the closing question of the short surah of the Fig at 95:8. In both places it stands at the end of a passage, and in both it is put as something the listener is expected to concede rather than debate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is answered by having its premise corrected, which is a distinct kind of answer. God does not refuse the request or reason with the grief; He tells Noah that the word he used does not mean what he assumed it meant. That makes prayer a place where a person's understanding can be adjusted, and it establishes that the promise held exactly, once household is defined the way the promise defined it.

crossReferences.why: Shows the shape of Noah's prayers elsewhere, including exactly whom he asks to have covered.
Shows another father taking his grief to God rather than to the people standing in front of him.
Closes a short surah with the same name, wisest of all who judge, put as a question.

studies.applyIt: When you next pray about something you badly want, try Noah's structure. Say what you believe is true about the situation, then what you believe is true about God, and stop there without joining the two into a demand. It is a small change and it does something specific: it leaves the connection between them open.

studies.title: Ask Me Not What You Do Not Know
studies.meaning: The answer comes in three parts and only the first concerns the son. He is not of your household, which redefines the word Noah had used. Then a phrase the commentators discuss at length, read either of the son's conduct or of the request just made. Then an instruction: do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of. The warning at the close is affectionate in its form and severe in its content.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This exchange is among the most discussed passages in classical commentary on the surah, and the discussion is grammatical rather than doctrinal, turning on whether the middle clause refers to the son, to his conduct, or to Noah's question. Al-Tabari records the range of readings and later commentators repeat it without resolving the matter.

keyTerms.note: The denial concerns belonging rather than descent. Commentators read it as redefining the word the promise had used, so that household in the covenant meant those who shared his faith.

keyTerms.gloss: an action that is not sound
keyTerms.note: A phrase whose reference is disputed. It is read of the son's conduct, of the son himself, or of the request Noah has just made, and the classical sources present all three without deciding.
The verb is of a warning delivered with concern, the kind a person gives someone they care for. It softens the correction while leaving it unmistakable, which is why it comes at the very end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kinship decided everything in Arabia and it was reckoned by blood. A man's obligations, his inheritance, his protection and his claim to vengeance all followed the family line, and no other criterion competed with it. Redefining a household by faith rather than by descent cut directly against the deepest organising principle the first listeners had.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the ignorant that closes this ayah is used across the Quran of behaviour rather than of information, including in the instruction at 7:199 to turn away from those who act ignorantly. Its appearance here, addressed to a prophet at the end of a mission lasting centuries, is one of the sharpest turns in the chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The correction establishes that belonging within the covenant is not inherited. That carries a consequence the surah has been building towards, since Mecca's leadership rested every claim it had on lineage. It also shows a prophet being told that he asked out of ignorance, which the passage neither hides nor treats as disqualifying, since the very next ayah is his response to it.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same limit with Abraham and his father, and names where the asking had to stop.
Uses the same word for the ignorant, in the instruction to turn away from them entirely.
States the general position: you have been given only a little of the knowledge there is.

studies.applyIt: There is probably something you have been asking God for that you have never examined. Not whether it is allowed, but whether you actually know it would be good. Take one such request today and add a clause to it, that you are asking without knowing. Nothing else about the request needs to change.

studies.title: Refuge From My Own Asking
studies.meaning: The response takes the correction and goes further than it had to. Noah does not defend his question or explain his grief; he asks for shelter from the act of asking itself, which turns a rebuke into something he takes on willingly. Then he names the stakes in the strongest terms available, and the commentators notice the vocabulary: it is the same commercial word for loss the surah used earlier of people who lost themselves entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the exchange over Noah's son. Commentators treat this ayah as the resolution of the episode and note that it arrives before the aftermath of the flood is described, so the reader leaves the scene holding the prophet's repentance rather than the drowning. That placement is read as deliberate rather than incidental.

keyTerms.note: The verb means attaching yourself to something for protection, the way a person clings to a strong post. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran, and here it is used against a fault the speaker has just been told about.

The root is that of covering, giving the words for a helmet and for a cloak. Forgiveness in this vocabulary conceals rather than erases, which is why it is requested alongside mercy rather than instead of it.

The commercial word this surah applied earlier to people who lost their own souls. Noah applies it to himself conditionally, placing himself in the same category as anyone else in the absence of forgiveness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seeking refuge was a formal act in Arabia. A man in danger could attach himself to a household or to a sanctuary, and the protection, once granted, bound the protector's honour even against his own kin. The phrase Noah uses belonged to that practice, so his prayer takes the shape of a fugitive claiming shelter rather than a servant offering an apology.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase Noah uses for seeking refuge appears three times in the Quran. The other two both fall in the twenty-third surah, where the Prophet is taught to seek refuge from the promptings of devils and from their presence. This is the only place the phrase is used about a question that has already been asked.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet is shown asking forgiveness for a request made out of love, which sets the standard high and at the same time makes it survivable. The passage does not treat the error as trivial, and it does not treat it as ruinous either; the remedy named is forgiveness and mercy, precisely what the surah has been telling Mecca to seek. The pattern applies to the messenger as much as to those refusing him.

crossReferences.why: Adam and his wife close with the same words: unless You forgive us we will be among the losers.
Records another prophet's admission inside a prayer made in the dark, and what followed it.
Shows Moses saying he wronged himself and asking to be covered, and being answered at once.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were corrected and answered by explaining why you had meant well. Explaining is not wrong, but notice what it does: it moves the conversation back onto your intentions. Today, when someone points something out, try accepting it in one sentence with no account of why, and see where the exchange goes instead.

studies.title: Come Down With Peace
studies.meaning: The landing is granted with two gifts and one warning. Peace and blessings come from God directly, and the blessings reach past Noah to communities that will descend from those aboard. Then the sentence turns: other communities will be given enjoyment and afterwards reached by a painful punishment. Commentators read this as the flood refusing to be a clean ending, since human history restarts carrying exactly the divided prospect it had before.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators observe that the ayah closes the Noah narrative not with vindication but with a forecast, and they connect that to the shape of the whole surah: four peoples destroyed, and the argument in Mecca still running. Peace is granted to one man, and a warning is attached to generations he will never meet.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used of Adam being sent down from the Garden. Its plain sense is descending from a height to a settled place, which makes the unloading of the vessel an arrival rather than a rescue.
The preposition makes the peace something he carries down with him. Naming its source removes any suggestion that safety was produced by the vessel or by the mountain it came to rest on.
The word names groups sharing a way of life rather than a bloodline. Used twice in one sentence with opposite prospects, it spreads the ayah forward over all the history that followed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Coming down was how Arabians spoke about arriving. A caravan descended from the passes into a valley settlement, and a traveller descended on a host, who then owed him protection and food. The formula of arrival mattered: guests announced themselves with peace, and a host answered with the same word before any business was raised.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated disembark here is the one used of Adam being told to go down from the Garden. It occurs seven times in the Quran, mostly of that first descent or of a comparable loss of place, and this is the only occasion where it is paired with peace and blessings rather than with departure from somewhere better.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is described as travelling forward rather than terminating in the rescue itself. Blessings reach communities not yet born, which turns the saving of a few people into an investment in generations. The warning attached to other communities stops the passage reading as a promise of permanent safety, and the two halves together present history as continuing under the terms it began with.

crossReferences.why: Closes the same story by leaving peace on Noah among all later people, and saving his family.
Uses the same verb of the first descent, and follows it with guidance offered on arrival.
Says the vessel and its company were saved and made into a sign for all peoples.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often relief arrives with a condition attached rather than as a clean ending. A treatment works and the follow-up begins; a debt clears and the habit that built it stays. Today, if something in your life has just resolved, resist calling it finished. Ask instead what the next part of it is actually for.

studies.title: Reports Of The Unseen
studies.meaning: The narrative stops and its purpose is stated openly. What has just been given belongs to what is absent from perception, and the point being made is evidential: neither the Prophet nor anybody around him held this information beforehand. Then an instruction, hold steady, and a promise about outcomes. Commentators note that the promise concerns the end of things rather than the middle, which is what makes patience the fitting response rather than confidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca had no written scriptures and no scholarly class, and what its people knew of earlier prophets came through travellers and traders. The claim made here was specific and testable at the time. Commentators note that the objection recorded against the Prophet in this period was that somebody had taught him, never that the accounts themselves were already common property.

keyTerms.note: The first word means significant news rather than any story, the kind that changes something on arrival. Joining it to the unseen marks the account as received rather than as gathered by inquiry.

The command follows from the narrative rather than from the hearer's circumstances. Having heard how long Noah waited, the instruction is being measured against that scale rather than an ordinary one.
From the root for a heel, what comes along behind. The word names what a thing turns out to be rather than how it looks now, which is why it can be promised while the present is going badly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories travelled Arabia by mouth and by caravan. Professional storytellers were known figures, and the great narratives of the older communities circulated in versions that shifted with the teller. A recitation giving a familiar name in an unfamiliar and internally consistent form would have been noticed at once by an audience that judged such things for a living.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase reports of the unseen occurs three times in the Quran, each time attached to a narrative the hearer could not have witnessed: this account of Noah, the account of who would take charge of Mary at 3:44, and the account of Joseph's brothers at 12:102. In all three the same point is made about not having been present.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns a narrative into an argument. What is offered as evidence is not the content of the stories but the fact of their arrival, which moves the question from whether the events happened to where the account came from. Attaching patience to the claim then does something further, presenting history as material for endurance rather than for curiosity.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase of a scene the hearer was not present at, and says so in the same breath.
Closes another long narrative with the identical formula about news the hearer did not witness.
Makes the point at length: you were not on the western side, nor by the Mount, when it happened.

studies.applyIt: Patience is being asked for here on the strength of a story rather than a promise about your week. Try reading one prophet's account from beginning to end today, in one sitting, without stopping to draw lessons. The scale is doing the work. It is difficult to keep a sense of urgency about six months while holding several centuries in mind.

studies.title: My Wage Is With My Maker
studies.meaning: The second narrative opens with a phrase this surah will use twice more: and to that people, their brother. Hud's demand matches Noah's, and so does his refusal of payment, but the reason he gives is his own. His wage rests with the one who originated him, which grounds the refusal in origin rather than in principle. Commentators observe the logic: a man collects his pay from whoever employed him, and Hud names his employer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were remembered in Arabian tradition as a people of the southern sands, associated with great building and with a strength no later people matched, and their disappearance had become proverbial before the Quran mentioned them. Hud is the first of the Arabian prophets named in this surah, and his story was the least foreign to its first hearers.

keyTerms.note: The word marks him as one of them by descent rather than an outsider. This surah applies it to three prophets in a row, which makes each refusal that follows the refusal of a relative.
The same root the Meccans used against the Quran earlier in this chapter. Here it is turned on those who manufacture gods, placing the charge of fabrication at the other end of the argument.

The root describes splitting something open, as a seed splits to grow. It is the Quran's word for creation as a bringing forth, and in this exact form it occurs three times, always inside a declaration of loyalty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The trade routes north from Yemen ran past ruins that Arabians attributed to vanished peoples, and travellers pointed them out in passing. A merchant on the incense road could see physical evidence that a great civilisation had stood there and was gone. Aad belonged to that landscape rather than to any book, which is why the name needed no introduction.
studies.didYouKnow: The prophet Hud is named seven times in the Quran, and five of those are in this surah, the only chapter that carries his name. The other two fall at 7:65 and 26:124, and in both places his opening words to Aad are given in nearly the same form they take here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Grounding the refusal of payment in origin rather than in ethics changes what it means. Hud is not saying that accepting money would be improper; he is saying that the one who made him is the one who owes him, which makes the whole transaction vertical. It also answers the natural suspicion of a man who speaks publicly, by removing every party who could have hired him.

crossReferences.why: Gives Hud's opening words to Aad in almost the same form, closing with a question instead.
Records the same refusal from him in different words: my payment is only from the Lord of the Worlds.
Recalls the brother of Aad warning his people at the dunes, with warners before him and after.

studies.applyIt: Think about who you are actually working for in one part of your life: a task at your job, something you do at home, a favour you keep repeating. Ask whether the return you are quietly waiting for is coming from that person. If it is not, and you would do the thing anyway, notice how much lighter the task becomes.

studies.title: Strength Upon Your Strength
studies.meaning: The two verbs this surah opened with are repeated word for word, and this time a specific promise is attached: rain in torrents, and strength added to what they already possess. Commentators read the second half carefully, since Aad were not weak, and the offer is of increase rather than of rescue. The closing prohibition then names the alternative not as unbelief but as turning away while carrying on as criminals.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed through a story to a city that also depended on rain and also had strength of its own. Aad are described elsewhere in the Quran as boasting about their power, and the classical commentators connect the promise of added strength to exactly that: the thing they were proudest of is offered back to them on different terms.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a root used of milk flowing freely from an udder. Applied to the sky it makes rain a kind of nursing, which is why the word turns up in promises rather than in descriptions of storms.
The repetition concedes what they already have before offering more. Commentators read the addition variously as numbers, as wealth, or as physical power, and note that the ayah declines to specify.
The word describes those who have cut themselves off from what is right. Placing it directly after turning away makes the two a single act, so departure and offence are named as one movement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in Arabia arrived within a few weeks and decided the year. A good season filled the valleys, greened the grazing, and let a tribe hold its territory without raiding, while a failed one emptied the wells and set families moving. Promising a sky that pours was promising the single variable everything else depended on, in terms every listener could price.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive word for pouring rain occurs three times in the Quran, and two of those are the same promise attached to the same condition: here in the mouth of Hud, and at 71:11 in the mouth of Noah, who adds wealth, children, gardens and rivers to it. The third occurrence describes rain sent to earlier peoples who were destroyed regardless.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A material promise is attached to repentance without repentance becoming a technique for obtaining it. Both prophets who use this formula are refused, and the surah records the refusals rather than any rain, which keeps the promise from reading as a mechanism. What it establishes instead is a direction: increase is described as coming from the same place forgiveness does.

crossReferences.why: Noah attaches the same promise to the same two verbs, adding wealth, children and gardens to it.
States the rule generally: had the towns believed, blessings would have opened from sky and earth.
Says whoever relies on God is provided for from where he never expected, and is sufficed.

studies.applyIt: The promise here is not that lack will be filled but that what you already have will be added to. Take one capacity you genuinely possess, some skill or patience or standing, and use it once this week on something that is not for you. That is closer to what the ayah is describing than asking for more of it.

studies.title: Not At Your Word
studies.meaning: The reply has three clauses and they move backwards. First a claim about missing evidence, then a refusal to act, then a flat statement of disbelief, which reverses the order anyone would use if evidence were genuinely the issue. Commentators note the phrase at your word: what is being refused is not a proposition but a man's say-so. The complaint about proof turns out to be the last thing added rather than the first thing withheld.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demand for a sign runs all through this surah, and commentators read the Aad narrative as exposing what that demand is for. Aad had received a messenger from among themselves, speaking their own language and known to them by name, and the objection they raise concerns his standing rather than anything in what he brought.

keyTerms.note: The same word Noah used of what he stood on. Denying that any of it arrived is a claim about what was presented, and the surah lets the claim stand without adjudicating what Hud had actually shown.
The construction names them as a type rather than reporting an action: we are not the sort of people who leave our gods. That makes the refusal an identity rather than a decision arrived at.
The preposition means as a result of. Naming his speech as the only cause on offer shows what the complaint about evidence really was, since a word is all any messenger in this surah brings.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inherited gods in Arabia were also inherited property. Shrines drew visitors, visitors brought trade, and the families who kept a sanctuary held their rank because of it. Abandoning a god was therefore not a private change of mind. It meant dismantling an arrangement that fed people, and everyone listening knew someone whose living depended on one.
studies.didYouKnow: Each of the four prophets whose stories fill this surah is addressed by name by his own people, and every time the vocative introduces a refusal: Noah at 11:32, Hud here, Salih at 11:62, and Shuaib twice, at 11:87 and 11:91. The pattern is unique to this chapter among the Quran's prophet narratives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the stated reason from the operative one. Evidence is named first and then abandoned immediately, since the next clause concedes that no evidence would have moved them: they are not the kind of people who leave their gods. The Quran records this without adding comment, which is its usual method of letting an argument reveal itself.

crossReferences.why: Says that even if the signs they swear by arrived, they still would not believe.
Preserves Aad's indifference in another form: it is all the same whether you warn us or not.
Records the same appeal to what the fathers were found doing, and the answer it receives.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the moment in your own arguments when you name a condition you would not actually accept: give me one example, show me the data, prove it. Ask yourself honestly whether the thing you asked for would change your mind. If it would not, say the real reason instead. It is a shorter conversation and a more honest one.

studies.title: Scheme Against Me, All Of You
studies.meaning: The accusation is offered as a diagnosis: one of our gods has struck him. Hud's answer does not argue with it. He calls two sets of witnesses, God and the people making the charge, and declares himself clear of everything they associate. Then he invites the attack. Commentators note the shape of the challenge, all of you together and without delay, which concedes both their numbers and their willingness while denying that either counts.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Attributing a man's strange behaviour to an offended god or an interfering spirit was ordinary explanation in that world, and the same charge was levelled at the Prophet. Commentators read Hud's response as a pattern for a messenger facing a whole community: no defence of his sanity, only a public disowning and an invitation to do their worst.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of an illness or a misfortune arriving on somebody unbidden. It frames Hud as afflicted rather than as wicked, which is a form of contempt dressed as concern for him.
The verb makes someone a witness formally. Calling both God and his opponents into the same role puts the declaration on record with the very people it is made against.
The root is of secret contrivance rather than open attack. Inviting it aloud strips away the concealment that makes such plotting work, which is what the challenge is actually doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who broke publicly with his tribe's gods lost his protection along with his religion. In practice that meant anyone could injure him without consequence, and his own kin would be under pressure to disown him rather than defend him. Inviting a whole people to scheme against him was inviting precisely the condition his society reserved for the unprotected.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Hud uses for declaring himself clear occurs nine times in the Quran, twice within this surah alone. One of the other occurrences is at 6:78, where Abraham uses it to disown the idolatry of his own people after watching the sun set. In every case it names a separation already complete rather than one being argued.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is redefined by being declined. Hud gives up the only shelter his society had to offer and asks for no substitute, and the following ayah names what he is relying on instead. The witnesses he summons matter too: putting God and his opponents in the same role means the declaration is made entirely in the open, which is how the Quran usually treats disowning.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham using the same word to declare himself clear of what his people associate.
Noah issues a comparable invitation: settle your affair together, and do not let it trouble you.
Gives Abraham and those with him as the example, renouncing their people and what they worship.

studies.applyIt: There is a particular relief in saying out loud the thing you have been half-hiding. Not an argument, and not a confrontation: one plain sentence about where you actually stand, said to someone who will not like it. Say it once this week without adding a justification, and notice that the dreading was heavier than the saying.

studies.title: He Holds It By The Forelock
studies.meaning: The reliance is stated and then given a reason, and the reason is a picture. Every creature is held by the forelock, the hair at the front of the head, which is exactly where a horse or a camel is taken to be led. Commentators note that this is the grip of someone guiding rather than crushing. Then a final clause that puzzles translators, read as saying that His dealing is upright, so the power just described is not arbitrary.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and one of the surah's central statements. Across these narratives the community around the Prophet is being told that safety comes from a source their opponents cannot reach. Hud says it at the moment he has just invited an entire people to plot against him, which is where the classical commentators locate the ayah's force.

keyTerms.note: From the word for the agent you hand your affairs to. The perfect tense makes it something already done rather than a resolution, so the sentence reports a completed transfer rather than a feeling.
The hair at the front of the head, where a mount is taken to be led. The word occurs in this form only here, and the image is of control exercised through guidance rather than through force.

The phrase familiar from the opening surah, applied here to God rather than to the worshipper. Commentators read it as saying His way of dealing is upright, which keeps absolute power from being arbitrary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel was managed from the front. The forelock was where a handler took hold to bring the animal's head down and turn it, and a raider who seized a mount by the forelock had it whether or not it wanted to come. Every listener had done this or watched it done, so the picture arrived complete before any argument was needed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for forelock appears in this exact form only here, but the same image returns at 96:15, where a man who forbids prayer is warned he will be dragged by the forelock. The identical grip is used once as reassurance to a threatened prophet and once as a threat to a man doing the threatening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah supplies the ground for reliance rather than simply commanding it. If every creature is already held, then the people plotting are themselves being led, which removes the question of odds entirely. The closing clause is what keeps the picture from being frightening, since a power that holds everything and deals justly is the only combination under which trust makes sense rather than mere submission.

crossReferences.why: Turns the same image of the forelock against a man who obstructs a servant from praying.
States the promise attached to this reliance: whoever relies on God, He will suffice him.
Records a threatened community answering mobilisation with the same posture: God is enough for us.

studies.applyIt: Reliance in this ayah is a completed act, not a mood. Pick one situation you have been carrying and say, once and in the past tense, that you have handed it over. Then behave for the rest of the day as though that were true: do your part of it, and stop rehearsing the parts that are not yours.

studies.title: I Have Delivered It To You
studies.meaning: The speech ends by settling accounts. The delivery is complete whatever they now do with it, and the verb chosen is the one for bringing something all the way to its destination. Then two consequences that are not about him at all: another people will be put in their place, and God is untouched by their refusal. Commentators note the order, since the replacement is stated as a fact about God's freedom rather than as a threat about their future.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Succession runs right through this surah: Aad are told here that they will be replaced, and elsewhere in the Quran they are reminded that they had themselves been made successors to the people of Noah. The commentators connect the passage to the Meccan leadership's working assumption that their standing in the city was simply permanent.

keyTerms.note: The verb means bringing something the whole way to where it was going. In the perfect tense it closes the messenger's account: the obligation was that it should arrive, and it has arrived.
From the root for a successor or a deputy. It describes replacement as the continuation of an office rather than an extinction, so the place remains and only its occupants change.

The word covers both protecting something and preserving a record of it. Applied to God over all things it means nothing goes unattended and nothing is mislaid, which is why it closes a speech about consequences.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Territory in Arabia changed hands. A tribe weakened by drought or defeat lost its wells and its grazing to another, and the newcomers took up the same valleys and the same routes, so the place outlasted the people. Aad were themselves remembered as having succeeded an earlier community. Hearing that the land would carry on without them described ordinary history.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Hud closes on, Guardian over all things, appears twice in this surah. Here it is affirmed of God, and at 11:86 Shuaib uses the same word to tell his own people that he is not a guardian over them. The identical term is denied of a prophet and asserted of God within one chapter, thirty ayat apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three claims are made and each takes something away from the audience. Their response does not affect whether the message was delivered, does not affect God, and does not secure their position. What is left to them is the choice itself, stripped of any leverage. Naming God as Guardian at the close then reframes the whole speech, since what is described is not indifference but a keeping that includes them.

crossReferences.why: Reminds Aad that they were themselves made successors after the people of Noah had gone.
States the same freedom: if He wills, He can remove you and put whom He wills in your place.
Warns that if you turn away He will replace you with another people who will not be like you.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you assume a place is yours: a role at work, a position in a family, a seat somebody always leaves for you. None of this is wrong to have. Just try holding one of them today as a loan rather than a possession, and see whether it changes how carefully you use it.

studies.title: They Followed Every Stubborn Tyrant
studies.meaning: The rescue is stated twice over, once as saving and once as delivering, and both are credited to mercy rather than to merit. Then comes the verdict on the people, naming three failures in ascending order: they denied signs, disobeyed messengers in the plural, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant. Commentators dwell on that last clause, since the fault named is not merely refusal but the substitution of one authority for another.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The plural messengers is discussed at length by the commentators, who generally read it as making the denial of one equivalent to the denial of all, since the message they carry is single. Aad were remembered as a people of exceptional strength, and the surah's account of them ends by naming what they were in fact following.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of a verb meaning to deliver from danger. The doubling across these two clauses, saved and then delivered, makes the rescue thorough rather than narrow, which is why mercy is named as its cause.
The plural is deliberate although only one messenger came to them. Commentators read it as making the message single across everyone who carries it, so refusing one is refusing the whole line.

The first word describes someone who forces others to his will, the second someone who resists what he knows. Together they name a leader both overbearing and knowingly wrong, and the pairing occurs once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe followed its chiefs in war, in alliance and in worship, and dissent inside a clan was closer to treason than to opinion. A man who broke ranks lost the group that fed and defended him. Naming the command of a stubborn tyrant as what Aad followed described a mechanism the first audience lived inside, not a foreign vice.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing for a stubborn tyrant occurs once in the Quran, here, though its second word appears three more times, always of someone resisting what he recognises. The Quran's account of Aad is unusually consistent in this respect: wherever they appear, the fault named is arrogance about strength rather than simple ignorance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verdict locates the failure in following rather than in believing. Aad are not described as having examined the message and rejected it; they are described as having taken their instructions from somewhere else. That makes obedience the operative category, and it places responsibility on both parties, since the tyrant is named and the people who followed him are the ones being addressed.

crossReferences.why: Names Aad's arrogance exactly: who is stronger than us, asked by people who forgot who made them.
Gives the same rescue by mercy from Us, and cuts off the roots of those who denied the signs.
Tells the same story at the dunes, ending with nothing left visible except their empty dwellings.

studies.applyIt: Look at whose judgement you have quietly adopted on something important: a view about money, about a group of people, about what a good life looks like. Trace it back and name the person. You may find you still agree with them. The exercise is worth doing because most of us have never checked whose ruling we are following.

studies.title: A Curse Sent After Them
studies.meaning: The consequence is described as something that follows rather than something that strikes. A curse was made to pursue them, in this life and again at the resurrection, which extends the sentence well past the destruction already reported. Then comes the formula of dismissal this surah uses four times. Commentators note the final phrase, since Aad are identified by the prophet they refused, so his name stays attached to them permanently.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah pronounces this dismissal over four peoples in turn, and the commentators treat the repetition as structural rather than rhetorical. Mecca's leadership traded on ancestry and on the memory of great forebears, so a formula that consigns an entire people to the phrase away with them was an argument about how names actually survive.

keyTerms.note: A passive of a verb meaning to send something after. The curse is not delivered to them but attached behind them, which is how it can reach into this world and the next at once.
The noun means being placed far off. Used here it names their condition rather than any utterance made against them, which is how the Quran generally handles the word.
A formula of dismissal built on the root for distance. This surah uses it four times, once over each destroyed people, and it appears only twice elsewhere in the whole Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation outlived people in Arabia. A tribe's standing was carried in verse, and poets kept both praise and satire alive across generations, so a family could still be defined by something an ancestor did centuries earlier. Being remembered badly was a real and feared outcome, which makes this closing formula a genuine sentence rather than a flourish.
studies.didYouKnow: The dismissal formula used here occurs six times in the Quran, and four of them are in this surah, once for each destroyed people: the people of Noah, Aad, Thamud and Median. The other two both fall in the twenty-third chapter. No other surah in the Book uses it more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage extends consequence past the event itself. Aad were already gone, and the ayah says the sentence continues to follow them, which separates destruction from judgement and treats the second as the more serious of the two. Naming them by their prophet does related work, since the relationship they refused becomes the thing they are permanently identified by.

crossReferences.why: Ends a different people with the same closing formula, away with the wrongdoing people.
Says a punishment of shame reached Aad in this life, with the hereafter's more shameful still.
Recalls Aad of the pillars, the like of which was never created in any land.

studies.applyIt: Think about what a person is remembered for, and how little of it they chose. Most reputations settle on one or two things a person did in public. Ask yourself what yours would currently be, and whether you would recognise it. You are not being asked to fix it today, only to look at it honestly once.

studies.title: Near And Answering
studies.meaning: The third narrative opens on the same pattern and adds an argument the others did not use. God raised you out of the earth and settled you on it to build, so the claim on you comes from origin and from tenure together. Then the familiar pair of verbs, and then two names. Commentators dwell on the second, which is given nowhere else in the Quran, and note that it turns an instruction into an assurance that the answer will come.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud were remembered in Arabian tradition as the people of the rock-cut dwellings along the northern trade route, and their ruins were visible to caravans travelling from Mecca towards Syria. Unlike Aad, who had simply vanished, Thamud left something a merchant could walk through, which commentators note when explaining why this surah uses them.

keyTerms.note: The verb describes bringing something into being and letting it grow, used of plants and of generations alike. It makes the human origin agricultural rather than manufactured, a raising up rather than an assembling.

keyTerms.gloss: settled you to build in it
keyTerms.note: The form carries being enabled or asked to do something. Its root gives words for cultivation, habitation and long life, so the sense is being handed the earth to develop rather than merely to occupy. It occurs once.

Two names in sequence, the second occurring nowhere else in the Quran. Nearness alone might be mere presence; adding the one who answers makes the closeness practical, which is why it follows an instruction to ask.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Thamud's dwellings were cut into rock faces, and Arabian caravans passed them on the road north. Travellers could see chambers and carved facades made by people nobody had met, standing empty in a landscape without water enough to support a city. The physical evidence of a people who had built well and gone was part of the ordinary route.
studies.didYouKnow: The name Answering, meaning the one who responds to a call, occurs only here in the whole Quran as a name of God. The verb behind it is used often of God answering prayer, but the name itself appears once, attached to the assurance that He is also near, inside a passage instructing a people to ask.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument from origin does something the other prophets' arguments do not. Salih grounds the demand for worship in a relationship that already exists, since these people were raised from the ground and settled on it long before any message reached them. The two names then answer the practical objection to repentance, that the request may go nowhere, by asserting proximity and reply in the same breath.

crossReferences.why: Answers the question about God's nearness in the same terms: I am near, I answer the one who calls.
States the nearness more sharply still: We are closer to him than his own jugular vein.
Gives Salih's opening to Thamud, and reminds them how they were settled in the land after Aad.

studies.applyIt: Two names are given here and they answer two different hesitations: that nobody is listening, and that nothing will come of it. Notice which of those actually stops you from praying. Then make one short request today, aloud, about something small and specific enough that you would notice an answer.

studies.title: We Had Hopes In You
studies.meaning: The refusal opens with a compliment, and that is the sharpest part of it. You were the one we placed our hopes in, said in the past tense, which tells us what he had been to them before he spoke. Then the objection, which concerns ancestors rather than God, and then doubt named with an intensifying word beside it. Commentators observe that the disappointment is genuine: they had expected him to take them further along the road they were on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the commentators connect the pattern to the Prophet's own position. He had been known in Mecca as trustworthy before the message came, and the leadership's complaint was of a man they had valued turning against the city's arrangements. Salih's people voice the same feeling, of a promising figure who had gone wrong at exactly the wrong moment.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle: he was the object of their hope, not the one holding it. The word occurs once in the Quran, and the past tense carries the weight, since what they had hoped for is never stated.
The verb of prohibiting, put as an incredulous question. It recasts a call to worship God as interference in something they were already doing, which shifts the whole argument onto their rights.
An adjective placed after the word for doubt, intensifying it. It names doubt that will not settle rather than an open-minded uncertainty, and it recurs later in this same surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A community's promising young man had a recognised role. He was the one groomed to speak for the tribe in disputes, to hold its memory, and to carry its arrangements into the next generation, and families invested in him accordingly. The complaint recorded here is not theological in origin. It is the complaint of people who had made plans around a man.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Thamud use for Salih, meaning one in whom hope had been placed, occurs only here in the Quran. The word they close on, for doubt that will not settle, occurs seven times, twice within this surah, so the same expression covers the doubt of Thamud and the doubt about the Book of Moses at 11:110.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a refusal made out of disappointment rather than out of conviction, which is a distinct category. What Thamud object to is not the existence of God but the disturbance of an inheritance, and they say so directly. The Quran preserves the objection in the form its speakers gave it, and the answer in the following ayah does not address the ancestors at all.
