crossReferences.why: Gives the same appeal to what the fathers were found doing, and asks what if they understood nothing.
Records the identical answer across peoples: we found our parents on a course and follow their footsteps.
Uses the same word for unsettling doubt, this time about a scripture given long before.

studies.applyIt: Somebody in your life has probably disappointed you by becoming more serious about something than you wanted them to be. That reaction is worth examining, because it usually reveals a plan you had for them that you never told them about. Name the plan to yourself today. You do not have to give it up to see it clearly.

studies.title: Who Would Shelter Me
studies.meaning: Salih answers their disappointment with a question about his own position rather than about theirs. Suppose the evidence is genuine: then who shelters him if he does what they are asking? The argument reverses the pressure, since compliance would put him in danger rather than in safety. His closing clause is blunt. Whatever they are offering, the net effect on him is subtraction, and the word he uses for that occurs only once in the whole Quran.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The formula opening this ayah is used by three different prophets in this surah, and here it introduces the sharpest version of the argument. Commentators connect the passage to the proposals put to the Prophet in Mecca, where various accommodations were floated in exchange for silence about the city's gods and its arrangements.

keyTerms.note: The verb is of coming to somebody's aid in a fight. Asking it about God rather than about enemies inverts the usual sense, since the danger named is the one his own compliance would create.

The root is that of a staff, and its verb came to mean resisting or striking out against authority. Salih applies it to himself hypothetically, which puts him under the same law he is calling them to.
A verbal noun from the merchant's word for a failed venture, occurring only here in the Quran. The form makes them the agents: they are not merely mistaken, they are actively costing him something.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a transaction. A man under threat sought a patron, and the patron's honour then stood between him and harm, so the whole social order rested on knowing whose protection covered whom. Salih's question uses that vocabulary exactly: if he offends the greatest party of all, which of them proposes to stand in the way?
studies.didYouKnow: The word Salih ends on, meaning the causing of loss, occurs only here in the Quran. Its root runs right through this surah, which reaches for the merchant's vocabulary of profit and loss four separate times, including of people who lost their own souls and of Noah fearing he would be among the losers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes obedience a matter of exposure rather than of preference. Salih is not saying that following them would be distasteful; he is saying it would leave him unprotected, which treats God's displeasure as the one danger no patron covers. Fear and hope are held together here, since the same clear evidence that makes him confident is what makes disobedience frightening.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical exposure in the Prophet's mouth: I fear, should I defy my Lord, a tremendous Day.
Answers a demand to alter the recitation with the same reasoning about disobeying his Lord.
Repeats the same personal fear of a horrendous Day, immediately before a statement of sincerity.

studies.applyIt: When someone asks you to compromise on something, the pressure usually arrives as a question about what it will cost you to refuse. Try asking the other question once today, about a small thing: what would it cost you to agree? People are much better at pricing refusal than agreement, and the second figure is often the larger one.

studies.title: Let Her Graze On God's Land
studies.meaning: The sign is an animal and the test is about sharing. She is called God's she-camel and the ground is called God's land, so the instruction is to let something feed where they had assumed an exclusive right. Commentators note that the Quran nowhere describes how she came, only what was to be done about her. The answer is a single verb, and then a countdown: three days, in their own houses, with the reliability of the notice stated outright.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud's country was arid and its water limited, and other accounts of this story specify that the she-camel had her own turn at the well. Commentators read the test as economic before it is theological: a whole community was asked to accept a permanent charge on a scarce resource, on the word of one man among them.

keyTerms.note: The construction assigns ownership. Calling the animal God's makes any injury to her a trespass rather than a loss of property, and the phrase occurs three times in the Quran, always in this story.
The command is to leave alone rather than to provide. What was asked of Thamud was restraint rather than generosity, which is a smaller thing to ask and evidently a harder one to give.
The verb describes cutting the leg tendons, the standard way of bringing a camel down. It is a deliberate, close-range act requiring a blade, so the ayah records a decision rather than an accident.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel at a well was a matter of order. Watering rights were divided into turns, and a beast that drank out of sequence could set families against one another; disputes over wells outlasted the people who started them. Being told that one animal held a standing claim on their land and their water was being told to accept a permanent inconvenience.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions the she-camel of Thamud in six different chapters and never once describes how she arrived. What it records instead is the instruction about her, the hamstringing, and the interval that followed. That is the usual shape of the Book's narrative interest: the choice rather than the marvel that occasioned it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test is built entirely out of restraint. Nothing is demanded except that something be left alone, which locates the failure precisely: Thamud did not refuse to give, they refused to refrain. The three-day interval afterwards does something else again, since a warning with a fixed term and a guarantee of accuracy leaves the time free for something other than surprise.

crossReferences.why: Specifies the arrangement they broke: she has her turn of drinking and you have yours.
Names the she-camel as a test sent to them, and tells Salih to watch and be patient.
Compresses the whole episode, from the warning about her to the levelling of the town.

studies.applyIt: The demand here was to leave something alone, which is a different discipline from giving. Pick one thing this week that you have a right to and simply do not exercise it: the last word in a disagreement, a parking space, a complaint you would be entitled to make. Notice that restraint costs a particular kind of effort.

studies.title: Saved From The Disgrace
studies.meaning: The rescue is described twice in one clause, from the event and from its shame, which the commentators treat as two separate deliverances. Being spared the disgrace of a day is not the same thing as surviving the day. Then two names close the ayah and both are names of power, which is a different ending from the passage on Aad and from the one on Median. The surah varies its closing formulas with some care.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The phrase introducing this ayah appears four times in the surah, once for each destroyed people, with the same structure of deliverance and mercy. Commentators note the small differences between the four and read them as fitted to each case: what Aad were told concerned succession, and what is said here concerns humiliation.

keyTerms.note: The word covers public shame and exposure rather than pain. Naming it as a second thing to be saved from implies that humiliation was counted as a distinct component of the punishment itself.
A name of capacity rather than of dominion. It answers a people whose own strength the Quran mentions repeatedly, and it is placed at precisely the point where that strength has just ended.

The root joins strength with scarcity and inaccessibility. It describes power that cannot be reached or resisted rather than power that merely prevails, which is why it usually stands beside another name.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shame was a public commodity in Arabia and it was inherited. A defeat was remembered in verse, and a family that lost standing could take generations to recover it, so avoiding disgrace often mattered more than avoiding loss. Being told that a group was saved from the shame of a day, and not only from the day, spoke directly to that priority.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah closes its four rescues differently each time, and the differences are not decorative. The account of Aad ends by naming the punishment they escaped as harsh, this one closes with two names of God, and the account of Median ends with no name at all, moving straight from the rescue to the sound that struck the town.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two names of power close a passage about deliverance, which is the reverse of what the content would suggest. The rescue was accomplished by mercy, and the ayah says so, then attributes the whole episode to strength and unassailability. Commentators read the pairing as guarding against a misreading: mercy here is exercised by one who could have done otherwise, not by one who was constrained.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same two names of God at the end of a passage about people driven from their homes.
Closes a declaration that He and His messengers will prevail with the identical pair of names.
Gives the same aftermath, and Salih's parting words to a town that could no longer hear.

studies.applyIt: Notice that being saved from humiliation is named here as its own gift. Think of a time you were spared not the loss itself but the public version of it, and nobody knew. That kind of protection is almost never noticed, because there is no story attached to it. Count one such occasion today as something you were given.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: As If They Never Thrived
studies.meaning: A people ends in one line and another story begins in the next. The Scream takes them and they are left settled and lifeless in their own houses, and then a clause does the real work: as if they had never flourished there. Commentators pause over that phrase, which erases not the people but the memory of their thriving. A few words later the messengers arrive at Abraham's door with good news, and the surah supplies no transition at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The abrupt junction here is deliberate, since the chapter moves from the erasure of Thamud straight into a scene of hospitality without pausing to comment. Commentators note that the visitors who exchange greetings with Abraham are on their way to destroy another town, so the good news and the next destruction travel in one party.

keyTerms.note: A single loud cry. The Quran uses it seven times as an instrument of destruction, twice within this surah, and it names a sound rather than a force, which is why the towns are left physically standing.
The word describes a body come to rest on the ground with its limbs beneath it, the posture of a camel kneeling. It gives the aftermath its stillness, since nothing is scattered or broken.

keyTerms.gloss: as if they had never thrived
keyTerms.note: The verb means being well off and settled in a place. The clause denies not their existence but their flourishing, so what gets erased is the prosperity rather than the people who held it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruined settlement was a familiar sight on Arabian routes, and travellers read them as they passed. Standing walls and empty cisterns told you a place had once had water and people, and the absence of both told you nothing about why. The phrase as if they never thrived describes exactly what a caravan sees at a site nobody now remembers.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause rendered as if they had never thrived occurs three times in the Quran, and two of them are in this surah: over Thamud here and over Median at 11:95. The third, at 7:92, is said of the people of Median again, so the phrase belongs almost entirely to the last two peoples this chapter destroys.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets an ending and a beginning beside each other without comment, which is how this surah handles time throughout. A whole civilisation's record closes in a single clause, and the next sentence is a man greeting strangers at his door. What the arrangement establishes is a proportion: what feels permanent from inside is, seen from outside, a paragraph.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same aftermath for Thamud, with Salih's parting speech to the ruined town.
Uses the identical clause of a different people, as if they had never prospered there.
Tells the story of Abraham's guests at greater length, with the same exchange of greetings.

studies.applyIt: Walk past a building today that was something else before, a shop that closed, an office that moved, a house that changed hands. Somebody organised years around that place. You are not being asked to feel bleak about it. Just register once, deliberately, how completely a thing can be over while its walls are still standing.

studies.title: Their Hands Did Not Reach
studies.meaning: The suspicion comes from a detail of hospitality. Their hands do not reach the food, and Abraham reads that as hostile, since a guest who will not eat has not accepted what a shared meal establishes. Commentators note that he conceals the fear and the ayah reports it anyway. Then the visitors name their errand, and while he is still absorbing it, his wife standing nearby laughs, and news of a son and a grandson arrives unasked.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators differ over the verb used of Abraham's wife, most reading it as laughter and some recording an older alternative, and they present the range without deciding between them. What they agree on is the order of events: the reassurance and the errand come first, and the good news follows without anyone having requested it.

keyTerms.note: The verb is of failing to recognise something as it ought to be. It names a mismatch rather than an emotion, which is why the fear has to be reported separately in the clause that follows.
A verb for something sensed faintly and privately rather than felt openly. It marks the fear as hidden, which is what makes the visitors' reassurance a disclosure of something he had not said.

keyTerms.gloss: so We gave her good news
keyTerms.note: The verb means news that shows in the face. In this form addressed to a woman it occurs once in the Quran, and the parallel accounts of this scene give the announcement to Abraham instead.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Eating together created obligation in Arabia. A guest who accepted food came under his host's protection and could not then be harmed by him, and a visitor who declined a meal was signalling that he had not entered that relationship. Abraham's alarm is not about manners. He is watching men refuse the one arrangement that would make them safe to have indoors.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the good news of a son is announced to Abraham's wife rather than to Abraham himself. The parallel scenes at 15:53 and 51:28 both direct the announcement to him, and only this account has her standing nearby, laughing, and being addressed in her own right.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes the moment a person is most afraid and turns it into the moment they are most given. Nothing has been asked for, and the fear is answered twice over, once by reassurance and once by an announcement reaching two generations forward. Commentators also note what the messengers do not do: they neither prove themselves nor explain, they simply say do not fear and state their business.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same scene with the fatted calf, the fear, and the wife's reaction in different words.
Gives the visit again, with the good news addressed to Abraham and his reply about old age.
Records the same errand, and Abraham's immediate objection that Lot is living in that town.

studies.applyIt: Abraham's fear was reasonable and he was wrong. Think of someone whose behaviour you have read as cold or hostile, and try assuming for one day that the signal you picked up meant something entirely different from what you assumed. You do not have to be right. You only have to notice how much you built on one detail.

studies.title: This Is A Strange Thing
studies.meaning: The reply is an exclamation before it is a question. She names the obstacle twice, her age and then her husband's, and the second is the more pointed, since it removes any possibility that the difficulty sits on one side alone. Then a verdict on the news itself: this is a strange thing. Commentators note that she is not doubting the messengers. She is registering a collision between what she has been told and what she knows about bodies.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The parallel account at 51:29 has her come forward crying out and strike her face, calling herself a barren old woman, and commentators read the two versions as the same reaction recorded from different angles. No occasion of revelation attaches to this ayah; it belongs to the narrative sequence the surah is carrying.

keyTerms.note: An exclamation of dismay rather than a complaint, closer to a cry of astonishment than to a sentence. It is a spoken sound first, which is why translators struggle to render it without making it sound formal.
The word is plain and unsoftened, the ordinary term rather than a respectful one. She applies it to herself, and that is what gives the line its unguarded directness.
The counterpart term, applied to her husband standing there. Naming both ages in a single sentence closes off the usual explanation for childlessness, since neither party is being held responsible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childlessness in a settled Arabian household was a permanent grief and a practical problem. Without sons, a man's land, herds and name passed sideways into a brother's line, and an old couple faced a future with nobody obliged to keep them. The astonishment here is not only biological. A whole expected ending is being cancelled.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this scene three times and each version preserves a different part of her reaction. Here she names both her age and her husband's; at 51:29 she cries out, strikes her face and calls herself barren; at 15:54 it is Abraham who asks how there can be good news when old age has already reached him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a reasonable objection stand without treating it as unbelief. She is not corrected for what she says, and the answer in the following ayah reframes the category rather than disputing her facts. That is a particular way of handling astonishment: the physical impossibility is conceded, and what gets denied is only that impossibility has the last word on what God decides.

crossReferences.why: Records her reaction in another form, and the answer that this is what your Lord has said.
Puts the same objection about old age in Abraham's mouth, and answers not to despair.
Shows Zechariah raising an identical difficulty about age, and being told it is easy for God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how quickly you rule things out on the basis of how things generally go. Most of that is sound judgement and you should keep it. But pick one thing you have written off as finished, and instead of deciding it might happen, simply stop stating that it cannot. That is closer to what this exchange is actually about.

studies.title: Blessings On This House
studies.meaning: The answer is a question followed by a statement, and neither of them addresses the biology. Do you find God's decree astonishing, they ask, which shifts the subject from what is possible to whose decision it is. Then mercy and blessings are declared over the household rather than over her alone, and the address turns plural. Commentators note that a private announcement has become a family one inside a single line.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The phrase people of the house is used here of Abraham's household, and it appears elsewhere in the Quran in other settings, which the classical commentators note without controversy. The scene belongs to the sequence of visits, and this greeting is delivered by messengers already on their way to destroy a nearby town.

keyTerms.note: The verb is addressed to a woman in the singular. It does not rebuke her; it asks whether astonishment is the fitting response to a decision, given who has been named as making it.
A term for a household, everyone belonging to a dwelling and its line. The address widens from one person to a family, which is what a promise of descendants actually concerns.

The first names one who deserves praise, the second one whose greatness is expansive and generous. Together they close the announcement with the character of the giver rather than the size of the gift.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household in that world was a unit with a future attached. It held its herds in common, married outward as a body, and was named after the man at its head, so a promise of children arrived as news about the entire establishment. Blessings pronounced over a house rather than over an individual were the ordinary form such things took.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close this ayah occur together in this exact pairing only here in the whole Quran. Each appears often on its own, and each is common in the formulas of praise recited in prayer, but the Book joins them in a single phrase once, at the end of an announcement made to a household.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply relocates the difficulty rather than solving it. Nothing is said about age or capacity, and instead the ayah asks whether astonishment is warranted once the source has been named, which turns the wonder into a question about what she assumed God's commands were subject to. Widening the address then does further work: mercy is described as landing on a household rather than on a body.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same answer in different words: so said your Lord, and He is the Wise, the Knowing.
Answers a comparable objection: it is easy for Me, and I created you before when you were nothing.
Records the same question about how, met with the reply that God does whatever He wills.

studies.applyIt: Good news usually gets delivered to one person and then rationed out. If something has gone well for you recently, tell the whole household at once rather than the person you most wanted to tell. The blessing in this ayah is pronounced over a group, and there is something in that shape worth copying.

studies.title: He Began To Plead With Us
studies.meaning: The sequence is what matters. First the fear leaves him, then the good news lands, and only then does he start arguing on behalf of a town that is not his own. Commentators note the timing: he pleads at the exact moment he has just been given something. Three adjectives then explain why, and the middle one is rare. After that the argument is closed from the other side, gently, with a reason supplied rather than a rebuke.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators discuss what Abraham's plea consisted of, since this passage gives only the fact of it, and they generally read it alongside the fuller version in another chapter where he objects that Lot is living in the town. What they emphasise is that the pleading is recorded with approval and stopped nonetheless.

keyTerms.note: The same verb Noah's people used against him earlier in this surah, meaning to argue at length. Applied to Abraham arguing with God on behalf of strangers, it carries no trace of reproach.

The quality of one who has the power to react and does not, holding back anger and postponing judgement. It is applied to God as well as to people, and it explains why Abraham argues rather than assenting.
A rare word for one who sighs or cries out from grief and tenderness. It appears twice in the Quran, both times of Abraham, and it names an emotional disposition rather than a moral virtue.
A participle of continuous action, describing someone whose default direction is towards God. It closes the trio by making the other two qualities habitual rather than occasional.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession was a recognised office in Arabia. A respected man would step between parties in a blood dispute, offering his own standing and often his own wealth to stop a killing, and such mediators were named and remembered for it. Abraham arguing for a town he does not belong to occupied a role the first audience recognised immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The rare middle word in this description of Abraham appears in only one other place in the Quran, at 9:114, where it also describes him, in the passage about his asking forgiveness for his father. It is used of nobody else, and both occurrences concern him pleading for people who will not in the end be spared.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage approves an argument that it also stops. Abraham's qualities are listed as the explanation for his pleading, which makes the impulse admirable, and then the plea is closed because the decree has already gone out. Both things are allowed to stand. What is established is that intercession has a place and also a limit, and that the limit is a matter of timing rather than of standing.

crossReferences.why: Gives the content of his argument, that Lot is there, and the reply that they know who is in it.
Uses the same rare word of Abraham, in the other passage where he pleads for someone unsparable.
Records the same exchange with the messengers, and the exception made for Lot's family.

studies.applyIt: Abraham argues at the moment he has just received something, not at the moment he needs something. Notice when you next get good news, and use some part of that hour on somebody else's problem rather than on your own plans. Relief makes people generous for about a day. It is worth spending deliberately.

studies.title: This Is A Dreadful Day
studies.meaning: The same visitors who brought good news to one house bring dread to another, and nothing about them has changed. Lot's distress is described with two expressions, one for being troubled by their arrival and one for a capacity narrowing to nothing, and both are about them rather than about himself. Commentators are careful here: what he dreads is his inability to protect guests, which in his society was among the worst things that could happen to a host.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators note that Lot did not yet know who these visitors were, so his fear is the ordinary fear of a man who cannot guarantee a stranger's safety inside his own town. The parallel accounts add that they appeared as young men, which the classical sources report and treat as the reason for his particular alarm.

keyTerms.note: A passive construction: the distress happens to him because of their arrival. It reports the effect rather than the emotion, which is why a second phrase is needed to describe how the effect felt.
An idiom built on the word for a forearm's reach. It describes running out of the ability to handle something, and Arabic still uses it of a person who has come to the end of their resources.
From a root meaning to bind tightly. It names a day that closes in around a person, and the phrase occurs only here in the whole Quran, in the mouth of a host expecting the worst.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality was the strongest obligation in Arabian life and the most publicly judged. A host was answerable for his guest's safety while the man was under his roof, and someone who let harm reach a visitor was disgraced for the rest of his life and often afterwards. Lot's dread was proportionate to a duty ranking above almost every other.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Lot uses for a hard day occurs once in the Quran. Its root gives the words for binding and knotting, and Arabic lexicographers explain the sense as a day tied so tightly around a person that nothing in it can be loosened. It is the strongest expression the Book uses for a bad day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a prophet's distress without qualifying it in any way. Lot is not shown as calm because he trusts God; he is shown narrowed to his limit, and the narrative simply continues from there. That establishes something about how the Quran presents its figures. Character here is measured by what a man is anxious about, and Lot's anxiety is entirely for people he has just met.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same arrival, and Lot's plea to the crowd not to disgrace him before his guests.
Records the identical distress on their account, with the reassurance not to fear or grieve.
Shows the messengers stating their errand to Abraham before they ever reach the town.

studies.applyIt: Lot's whole distress is about somebody else's safety. Ask yourself what you were last genuinely worried about, and whether the answer was a person or an outcome that concerned you. Neither is shameful. But if it has been a while since the answer was somebody else, that is worth noticing about the shape of a week.

studies.title: Not One Reasonable Man
studies.meaning: The crowd is described as being driven forward, and then a clause explains that this was nothing new for them. Lot's response includes an offer that commentators read in more than one way, some taking the daughters literally and some reading it as the women of the community, whom a prophet may address as his daughters. What is not disputed is the last line: he searches the crowd for one man of sound judgement and does not find him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators discuss Lot's offer at length and record the range of readings without settling it. The episode is told here as one item in a sequence of destroyed communities, and this surah's interest is in the town's overall condition rather than in any single act, which is why the crowd's established habit is mentioned before anything they say.

keyTerms.note: The form suggests being urged forward rather than choosing to run. It occurs twice in the Quran and gives the crowd the quality of something moving by momentum rather than by anyone's decision.
From the root for shame and exposure. Lot asks them not to shame him in front of guests, which places his appeal inside the one obligation his town still recognised as binding.
The adjective describes someone whose thinking arrives in the right place. It occurs three times in the Quran, all three in this surah, twice as a compliment and once as an outright denial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A town's elders were expected to contain a crowd. Someone with standing would step out, name the men he recognised, and take responsibility for calming them, and the whole social order depended on such people existing. Lot's question is a search for that man, and its force lies in the fact that everyone listening knew such a person was supposed to be there.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Lot uses for a right-minded man occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah. Here he asks whether even one exists; at 11:87 the people of Median call Shuaib forbearing and right-minded, apparently in sarcasm; and at 11:97 the command of Pharaoh is said to be anything but right-minded.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah measures a community by whether it still contains one person capable of judgement. That is a different test from counting the wicked, and this surah returns to it later, at the point where it asks why earlier generations produced no people of discernment to speak against corruption. What ruins a town in this chapter is the absence of anyone left willing to object.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question to history: why were there no people of discernment forbidding corruption.
Gives the same crowd, the same appeal about his guests, and the same offer of his daughters.
Records Lot's charge against the town and his prayer for help against a corrupting people.

studies.applyIt: In any group going in a bad direction, the useful person is rarely the loudest objector. It is whoever is willing to say the plain thing once, calmly, while everyone else is committed. If you are in such a group this week, be that person for one sentence. You do not have to win. You have to exist.

studies.title: If Only I Had A Pillar
studies.meaning: The refusal is put as a fact about him: you know. Said twice. What they reject is not the offer but the pretence that the offer addresses anything at all. Lot's answer is not an argument; it is a wish, and it names two things he lacks, personal force and a strong support to fall back on. Commentators note that the second is the more telling of the two, since what he is missing is a clan rather than muscle.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Lot was a stranger among the people of his town, having travelled there with Abraham from elsewhere, which is why he had no kin group standing behind him. Commentators read his wish for a strong support in precisely that light, and several report words attributed to the Prophet expressing sympathy for Lot at this moment.

keyTerms.note: An emphatic construction carrying two particles of confirmation. Said to him twice, it removes any possibility of misunderstanding and turns their intention into something openly acknowledged on both sides.
The ordinary word for physical or numerical power. Lot names it first because it is what a man standing alone would need, and its absence is what makes the second half of his sentence necessary.
The word means the corner or supporting pillar of a building, used figuratively of a clan that holds a man up. The phrase occurs only here, and it names social backing rather than personal courage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man without a clan in Arabia was structurally unsafe. Protection came from relatives who would avenge him, and a resident outsider survived by attaching himself to a local family who agreed to cover him. Lot is describing that exact deficit: not weak arms, but nobody behind him who would make an attack on him expensive to attempt.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Lot wishes for, a strong pillar, occurs only here in the Quran. Its root returns thirty-three ayat later in this same surah, at 11:113, where the listeners are told not to lean towards those who do wrong. The same image of leaning on something serves once as a longing and once as a warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a prophet say he is not strong enough, and adds no correction to it. No help arrives inside this ayah and no reassurance is offered until the next one, so the admission is allowed to stand on its own for a moment. What the sequence establishes is that the help came after the acknowledgement of helplessness rather than instead of it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root for leaning, warning the listeners not to incline towards those who do wrong.
Gives the same exchange, with his plea about the guests and the crowd's flat reply.
Records that he had warned them, that they disputed it, and what happened to their sight.

studies.applyIt: There is a specific relief in admitting you cannot handle something, and most of us delay it until the situation forces the words out. If you are currently past your capacity in some area, say so out loud today to one person who can hear it. Lot said it with nobody there at all, and help arrived in the next breath.

studies.title: Is Not The Morning Near
studies.meaning: The identity is disclosed at the moment it is needed and the instructions follow at once. Travel in a portion of the night, let nobody look back, and one person is excluded from the departure. Then the timing: their appointed hour is daybreak. The ayah ends on a question that is not really a question, put to a man who has just been told to walk through the dark. Commentators read it as consolation about how short the waiting will be.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators read the closing question as addressed to Lot's exhaustion rather than to any doubt of his, and several connect it to the surah's wider instruction to the Prophet to hold steady. A community waiting in Mecca is shown a night that has a stated end, and a man told to walk the length of it.

keyTerms.gloss: in a portion of the night
keyTerms.note: The noun means a piece cut from something, so the night is treated as a length to be measured out. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran, and both are this same instruction given to this same man.
The verb is of turning the face back over the shoulder. It prohibits the specific movement rather than the feeling behind it, which is how the classical commentators read the instruction.
The noun names an appointment already fixed rather than a threat being issued. Setting it at dawn also fixes the length of the walk, since the night they cross is exactly the time remaining.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel was standard in Arabia and it was also dangerous. Caravans moved after dark to spare the animals and avoid the heat, navigating by the stars, and a family leaving a town at night without an escort was doing something recognised but risky. Being told to go by night, with dawn as the deadline, was a route and a clock at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for travelling in a portion of the night occurs twice in the Quran, and both are the same instruction to the same man: here, and at 15:65, where he is told to travel at the dead of night, to follow along behind his family, and to let none of them turn to look back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The messengers answer the previous ayah's wish without ever commenting on it. Lot said he had no strength and no support, and the reply is simply that they will not reach you, which supplies the missing pillar directly. The closing question then reframes the night itself: the waiting is real, it is being asked for, and its length has already been fixed by the one who set the appointment.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in nearly identical words, with the same prohibition on looking back.
Names the same exception for his wife, and gives the same reassurance not to fear or grieve.
Records his prayer for deliverance, and the saving of all his family except one who remained.

studies.applyIt: The last line of this ayah is a fact offered as comfort: the morning is close. If you are in the middle of something you are counting down, try saying the actual remaining number out loud once today, the weeks or the days. Vague endurance is heavier than measured endurance, and the difference is usually just arithmetic.

studies.title: Never Far From The Wrongdoers
studies.meaning: The destruction is given in two verbs and one detail. The town is inverted, and then stones of a hardened clay fall on it, described as marked. Commentators read the marking variously, as designating particular targets or as showing these were no ordinary stones, and they record the readings. The last clause then leaves the story altogether: such a thing is never far from wrongdoers, which addresses the listener rather than the town.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the closing clause is where the commentators locate the address. Mecca's caravan route north to Syria passed near the sites traditionally identified with these towns, so the Prophet's opponents travelled through the region regularly. Several commentators read the final phrase, that it is not far off, with that geography in view as well as the moral sense.

keyTerms.note: A construction naming the inversion without any verb of destroying. What is described is a reversal of position rather than a demolition, which is why translators reach for turned upside down.

A word for stone baked from clay, used three times in the Quran and always of stones sent down. Lexicographers debate whether it is originally Arabic or borrowed, and the classical sources record both views.
A participle for things stacked one upon another. The Quran uses it twice, once of these stones and once of clustered trees in the Garden, so the same word covers a punishment and a reward.
From a root for a distinguishing sign, used elsewhere of branded horses. Commentators read the marking either as identifying each stone's target or as showing they came from beyond ordinary weather.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Volcanic fields lie across parts of northern Arabia, and the road to Syria crossed beds of dark, porous rock unlike anything in the Hijaz. Travellers knew that ground was strange and that the region held ruins nobody claimed. A description of baked stones falling on an overturned town matched a landscape merchants had actually crossed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing these stones as layered occurs twice in the Quran. Here it describes what falls on the town; at 56:29 it describes the clustered trees of the Garden. The same participle serves for something stacked in punishment and something stacked in reward, and it is used nowhere else in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The final clause is what makes this more than a record. Having described a specific destruction in specific detail, the passage refuses to leave the matter in the past and says the thing is never far from wrongdoers. That is a statement about proximity rather than about certainty, and it converts a historical account into a live one without predicting anything at all.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same destruction at dawn and calls what remained a sign for those who read signs.
Names the messengers' errand and calls the stones marked by your Lord for the excessive.
Uses the same baked stones much later, against an army that approached the sanctuary itself.

studies.applyIt: The last line moves the whole account into the present tense. Read this ayah and then look at something you have filed away as belonging to a different kind of person or a different era. Ask what the nearest ordinary version of it looks like where you actually live. That is what the word near is doing here.

studies.title: Do Not Cut The Measure
studies.meaning: The fourth narrative opens on the established pattern and adds a second demand at once. Worship God, and do not cut the measure or the weight, so a commercial practice is named in the same breath as belief. Commentators note the observation that follows: he sees them well off, which is not a compliment but a diagnosis, since prosperity is what the shortfall has bought. The day he fears is then described as encompassing, closing in from every side.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Median lay on the trade route north, and its people were merchants and caravan handlers, which is why the fault named is a commercial one. Commentators note the fit with this surah's first audience: Mecca lived on the same trade, and the practices Shuaib names would have been recognised in its own markets without any translation.

keyTerms.note: The dry measure used for grain and the scale used for weight, the two instruments of every market. The pair occurs twice in the Quran and both times in this surah, in consecutive ayat.
The word means good in the widest sense, prosperity included. Naming their comfort immediately before naming the day makes the observation a warning rather than an approval of their success.
A participle for something that surrounds on every side. Applied to a day it removes any edge to escape from, and this surah later uses the same word of God's knowledge of what they do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A market ran on trust in its instruments. Grain was sold by a standard measure and metal by weight, and a merchant who shaved either could profit for years without a single customer noticing. Towns appointed inspectors precisely because the fraud was invisible, and everyone listening knew the honest trader and the dishonest one looked identical from outside.
studies.didYouKnow: The measure and the balance are named together twice in the Quran, and both occurrences fall in this surah, in this ayah and the one directly after it. Elsewhere the same fault is described in other terms, but only here does the identical pair of market instruments appear twice in consecutive ayat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing worship and honest weighing side by side makes them one demand rather than two. The passage does not derive the second from the first or present commerce as an application of belief; it names them together, which is how this surah handles the relation throughout. The word chosen for the day then answers the specific comfort of a fraud, which depends entirely on not being seen from every angle at once.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same opening to Median, with the identical instruction about measure and weight.
Describes the practice exactly: full measure taken, short measure given, before a great day.
Sets the balance in the sky and tells people not to violate the one they hold in their hands.

studies.applyIt: The fault here is invisible by design: nobody feels a measure that is slightly short. Look for your own version this week, the place where you deliver slightly less than you agreed and nobody could tell. Fix that one, quietly, without announcing it. The whole point of the fault is that no correction will ever be noticed either.

studies.title: What God Leaves You
studies.meaning: The instruction is restated positively and then widened twice. Give in full, do not shortchange people in anything at all, and do not go about corrupting the land, so a market fault becomes a public one inside a sentence. Then a phrase commentators discuss at length: what remains from God is better for you. And then Shuaib steps back, saying he is not a keeper over them, which leaves the decision where it started.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators read the widening of the charge as significant, since Median's problem is described as beginning in the measure and ending in the land, which is how the Quran generally treats a practice a whole society has adopted. Shuaib's disclaimer at the end echoes instructions given to the Prophet during the same period.

keyTerms.note: The verb of giving less than what is owed, used earlier in this surah of a payment that will not be shorted. It covers goods, wages and rights alike, so the prohibition reaches well past the market.
A phrase found once in the Quran. Commentators read it either as the lawful profit remaining once fraud is given up, or as the reward held with God, and they set both readings side by side.
The same word this surah applies to God twenty-nine ayat earlier. Denying it of himself marks the boundary of a prophet's role: he delivers the message and he does not supervise the response.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Corruption in the land had a concrete meaning on a trade route. Median sat where caravans passed, and a town that cheated travellers eventually lost them, taking the wells, the guides and the whole economy of the road down with it. Shuaib's warning about the land was not a metaphor. It described what happens to a place that gets a reputation.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for what God leaves you occurs once in the Quran, but its root turns up twice more in comparable settings, at 18:46 and 19:76, where the enduring good deeds are called better with your Lord than wealth and children. This surah uses the same root again at 11:116, of the people of discernment a society ought to have kept.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes honesty a matter of accepting a smaller amount. What is left once you stop taking what is not yours is described as better, which reframes the loss as the actual gain, and the argument is offered conditionally, if you are believers. Shuaib then withdraws his own authority in the same breath, so the instruction stands with no enforcer attached to it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to Median and adds not to spoil the land after it was set in order.
Uses the same root: the deeds that last are better with your Lord in reward and in hope.
Repeats the measure, the balance, and the wider charge not to work corruption in the land.

studies.applyIt: Try the arithmetic this ayah proposes. Take something you gain by a small unfairness, the extra hour claimed, the corner cut, the price not quite explained, and calculate what you would have without it. It is almost always a smaller number that you could live on comfortably. The word better in this ayah is doing real work.

studies.title: Does Your Prayer Command You
studies.meaning: The objection is put as a question about where his authority comes from, and it names his prayer. Commentators note the sneer in that: they are asking whether a private devotion has begun issuing him public instructions. Two demands are then lumped together, the ancestors and the money, which shows how the two were held. The compliment at the end is read by most commentators as sarcasm, though a minority take it straight.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators observe how closely this objection matches the one recorded from Mecca's leadership, whose complaint was that a man's religion had started interfering with trade and with inherited practice. Naming his prayer in particular suggests Shuaib was known for it, which the classical sources note in passing without elaborating.

keyTerms.note: The question opens with a particle of astonishment attached to the word for prayer. This exact form occurs once in the Quran, and it makes a devotional act into the alleged source of a public demand.
The verb of issuing an order, applied to his prayer as though it were a person. The construction is what carries the mockery, picturing him taking instructions from his own act of worship.
Two compliments carrying the definite article, which most commentators read as sarcasm. The second word occurs three times in the Quran, all in this surah, and only here as apparent praise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in a trading town was not merely private property; it was a family's standing and its dependants' security. What to do with it was among the last things any man would concede to an outsider. Pairing that with the worship of ancestors, inside a single question, shows exactly how the two were held: as parts of one inheritance.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where anyone asks whether a prophet's prayer is what commands him. The exact form of the question occurs once, and it is put by people objecting to two things in the same breath: an inherited religion, and their freedom to do whatever they like with their own money.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The objection is more revealing than its speakers intend. They identify the prayer as what generates the demands, which is a fair description of where a prophet's instructions come from, and they pair worship with property as a single sphere they will not have interfered with. The Quran records the complaint without correcting it, since the connection they resent is a real one.

crossReferences.why: Says prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing, which is precisely the interference they resent.
Records Median's leadership threatening eviction unless he returns to their religion.
Gives Shuaib's demands again, with the same instruction about measure, weight and corruption.

studies.applyIt: They were right that his prayer was changing what he asked of them. Ask whether yours changes anything you do outside it. Not whether it should, but whether it currently does. If nothing comes back with you from the prayer into the rest of the day, that is worth sitting with for a minute before you try to fix it.

studies.title: I Want Nothing But Repair
studies.meaning: This is Shu'ayb's answer to a community that told him to stop interfering with their trade. He does not argue about the practices. He puts a question about his own position. He claims clear evidence and honest livelihood. Then he makes a specific promise: he does not intend to do privately what he tells others not to do. The aim he names is repair, limited to what he can manage. The speech ends by handing the outcome over.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside a sequence of prophets told one after another in this surah. Shu'ayb is sent to the people of Madyan. It was a trading community on the caravan route north. The dispute concerns short measures, and interference with what people did with their own property. Early scholars treat the exchange as the surah's fullest account of an argument about trade rather than about worship alone.

keyTerms.note: Something that makes a matter plain, from a root for separating and clarifying. It names a basis he claims to be standing on rather than a wonder he is offering to perform for them.
From the verb to mend what is broken, used of reconciling people and of restoring a thing to working order. It is the exact opposite of the word the Quran uses for corruption in the land.
From a root for agreement and for things fitting together. It names success as a match between a person's effort and what God allows, which is why it cannot be claimed as an achievement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Madyan sat on the trade route between Arabia and Syria. Its wealth came from handling other people's goods. Measures and weights were the tools of that business. A merchant with a shaved weight could take a fraction from every deal for years without being caught. The community's objection was that a religious teacher had opinions about the scales.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause in which he says he does not want to do himself what he tells others to avoid is unusual in the Quran. Prophets rarely defend their own conduct there. Classical scholars note that the charge being answered is hypocrisy rather than error. He meets it with a statement of intention rather than with evidence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out what a person calling others to change may claim and what they may not. Evidence and honest provision are claimed; results are not. Limiting the aim to what he is able to do removes the pretension from reform, and handing success over to God removes the credit for it. Between them those two clauses describe a way of trying to improve things that does not depend on succeeding.

crossReferences.why: States plainly how hateful it is to say what you do not do.
Gives the instruction about full measure that this speech is defending.
Asks whether people enjoin righteousness on others and forget themselves.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have advised someone else to do in the last month and check whether you are doing it. If not, either do it this week or stop giving the advice. Shu'ayb answers a charge of hypocrisy by naming his intention, and the only way to keep that claim honest is to check it against something specific.
studies.explainEasier: Shu'ayb told his people he was not asking them to do anything he would not do himself. He only wanted to put things right, as far as he could. He left the rest to God.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: Merciful And Loving
studies.meaning: The warning is built out of the surah itself. Three peoples are listed in the order this chapter told them, and a fourth is added with a remark about distance, which commentators read as geographical, or chronological, or both. Then the formula the surah has already used twice, and this time it closes on two names of God. The second is rare, and it is the last word of the whole appeal.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Median lay nearer to the territory of Lot's people than to the others named, which is why commentators discuss whether the closing remark about distance refers to place or to time. The list itself works as a summary, since by this point the surah's audience has been given each of these accounts at length.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to break a thing into two sides, so the word names a rift rather than an emotion. Shuaib warns that the division itself may cost them, putting the danger in the standoff rather than in him.

keyTerms.gloss: let it not drive you to
keyTerms.note: An emphatic prohibition from the root behind the word for crime. It pictures hostility as something that carries a person into a consequence he never deliberately chose.
An intensive form from a root for affection that shows itself in action. It occurs twice in the Quran as a name of God, and here it closes an appeal to people just reminded of four ruined towns.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia acquired their own momentum. A quarrel begun over a specific injury could outlive its cause and settle into a standing hostility neither side could end without losing face, and whole clans were ruined by disputes nobody could remember the start of. Shuaib names precisely that mechanism: the split itself doing the damage.
studies.didYouKnow: The name Loving occurs twice in the whole Quran, here and at 85:14, where it stands beside the Forgiving. Both times it appears at the end of a passage about severe punishment, so the Book places its most intimate name for God in exactly the two contexts where a reader would least expect it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The appeal joins a list of destroyed peoples to a name of affection, and the joining is the entire point. Having named four catastrophes, Shuaib does not finish with a threat but with the assertion that the one who did those things is merciful and loving. Commentators read the pairing as the surah's summary position, that warning and invitation are one act addressed to the same people.

crossReferences.why: The only other place this name appears, standing immediately after a passage about burning.
Says the Merciful will appoint love for those who believe and do righteous deeds.
Records the threat Median made in reply, and Shuaib's refusal to return to their way.

studies.applyIt: Notice which name you finish on when you think about God. Most of us have a default, and it is usually formed early and rarely revisited. Read this ayah tonight and let it end where the ayah ends rather than where the list of ruined towns ends. The order in the sentence is not accidental.

studies.title: Were It Not For Your Kin
studies.meaning: Three statements, and every one is about position rather than about content. We do not grasp much of it; you are weak among us; only your family is stopping us. The last clause states the calculation openly, that he holds no standing they need respect. Commentators note the admission buried inside the third sentence, since they concede that a household they otherwise never mention is the only thing keeping a prophet alive.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the parallel is exact. The Prophet was protected during these years by his own clan, and the classical accounts describe the leadership's frustration at being unable to move against a man they otherwise disregarded. Commentators read the passage as recording a situation the first audience knew from both sides of it.

keyTerms.note: The verb means understanding something through rather than merely hearing it. Claiming not to grasp is a stronger dismissal than claiming not to agree, because it locates the failure in the speaker.
The ordinary word for physical or social weakness. Classical reports differ over whether it points at his eyesight, his numbers, or his lack of a strong faction, and commentators record the range.
A word for a small band of relatives, fewer than ten by some accounts. It occurs once in the Quran, and its smallness sharpens the point: even a minor clan was enough to stop them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood revenge made violence expensive. Killing a man obliged his relatives to answer, and the cost of the feud that followed was reckoned before anybody acted, so a small clan willing to retaliate protected a member far better than his own strength ever could. Median's leaders are stating that arithmetic aloud, without any embarrassment about it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Median use for Shuaib's relatives occurs once in the Quran. It denotes a very small group of kin, and lexicographers give figures under ten. The insult and the confession sit inside one sentence: he is worthless to them, and a handful of his relatives is the only thing preventing his death.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a protection working through an ordinary social mechanism rather than through a miracle. Nothing intervenes; a small family is simply present, and that turns out to be enough. Commentators note this as characteristic of how the Quran describes God's arrangements in these narratives, which generally operate through the material means available rather than by suspending them.

crossReferences.why: Gives Median's threat of eviction and the warning issued to anyone who might follow him.
Records the same dismissal in another town: you are only humans like us, and you are lying.
Adds their demand that pieces of the sky be dropped on them if he is truthful.

studies.applyIt: Somebody is probably protecting you in a way you have never counted: a manager who absorbs criticism, a relative whose name opens a door, a friend who talks about you well when you are not there. Work out who that is for you, and say thank you for the specific thing this week rather than in general.

studies.title: Put Behind Your Backs
studies.meaning: The reply picks up their own word and turns it into a question about ranking. You restrained yourselves for my relatives; is a handful of men weightier with you than God. Then an image: they have put Him behind their backs, discarded like something set aside and forgotten. Commentators note the closing clause, which uses the same word the surah applied earlier to a day that encompasses, this time of God's knowledge of their conduct.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators treat this exchange as the clearest statement in the surah of what these prophets were actually contesting. Median's leadership had not denied God; they had ranked Him below the practical considerations that governed their decisions, which is exactly what the question here brings into the open.

keyTerms.note: The comparative is built on the root for might and inaccessibility, which is a name of God elsewhere in this surah. Asking whether a few relatives outrank Him puts the comparison in the starkest available terms.
An idiom for something thrown behind the back and forgotten, built on the word for a back. It occurs once in the Quran and describes neglect that is deliberate rather than absent-minded.
The same participle used earlier in this surah of a day that surrounds from every side, applied here to God's knowledge of their conduct. The repetition ties the warning and the knowing together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was measured concretely in that world: the number of men who would come out for you, the alliances your family held, the debts owed to it. When Shuaib asks whether his small clan outweighs God, he is using a scale everyone present computed daily. The question is not rhetorical to them. It is a comparison in familiar units.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for casting something behind the back occurs once in the Quran. Its root is the ordinary word for a back, and Arabic uses the idiom for a thing put deliberately out of sight rather than merely overlooked, which is why translators reach for expressions like thrown away and turned your backs on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a form of unbelief that has nothing to do with denial. Median believed enough to be told they had turned their backs, and what is charged is a matter of ranking rather than of doctrine. That makes worship in this surah a question of what actually restrains a person, and the answer Median gives, without meaning to, is a small family with a reputation for retaliation.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question of ranking: parents, children, wealth and trade set against God and His messenger.
Uses a comparable image of a group throwing the Book of God behind their backs.
Closes with the same word, that He encompasses every single thing there is.

studies.applyIt: Work out what actually stops you doing something you would otherwise do. For most people it is being seen, or a specific person's reaction, rather than any principle. Name yours honestly today. Not to feel bad about it, but because Shuaib's question only works on someone who knows the real answer to it.

studies.title: I Am Watching With You
studies.meaning: The argument ends in a standoff stated without hostility. Work from where you stand and I will work from where I stand, and afterwards it will be clear which of us was lying. Commentators note that the question left open is not who is right but who is untruthful, which is the charge that had been laid against him. Then a final instruction to keep watch, and the last word is that he is watching too.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This formula appears twice in the surah, here in Shuaib's mouth and again near the end, where the Prophet is instructed to say almost the same thing to his own opponents. Commentators treat the repetition as deliberate: the chapter gives the words to a prophet inside a narrative and then hands them to the one reciting it.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb to be, so it means the standing a person occupies. The phrase appears four times in the Quran, twice in this surah, and always in a formula of parting ways.
The specific charge Median had levelled at him. Framing the outcome as a test of who lied, rather than of who was correct, keeps the standoff on exactly the ground the objectors themselves chose.
From a root for observing from a height, used of a sentry on a ridge. The imperative is given to them and then claimed by him in the same breath, so both parties end up posted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A watchman on high ground was how a settlement stayed alive. Somebody kept the ridge for approaching dust, and the whole community's safety depended on his attention through the night. Telling opponents to take up that watch, and saying he would keep it alongside them, put both sides in the same posture facing the same horizon.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula translated do as you may occurs four times in the Quran, and two of them are in this surah: here in Shuaib's mouth to Median, and at 11:121, where the Prophet is instructed to say the same words to those who do not believe. The chapter gives the sentence to a prophet and then repeats it to its own reciter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models a way of ending an argument that neither concedes nor escalates. Shuaib does not restate his case, threaten, or claim victory; he names what the outcome will settle and then takes up the same watch he assigns to them. That places both parties in front of an event neither controls, which is the position this surah has been arguing for from its opening.

crossReferences.why: Gives the Prophet nearly the same words to say, and adds that both sides are now waiting.
Records the identical formula, with the outcome named as whose the final home will turn out to be.
Repeats it again, followed by the question of who receives a punishment that disgraces him.

studies.applyIt: Some disagreements cannot be settled by more talking, and the honest move is to say so. If you are in one, try Shuaib's ending: state plainly what would eventually show which of you was right, and then stop arguing. Not as a threat, and not as a sulk. As a description of where the matter actually rests.

studies.title: By A Mercy From Us
studies.meaning: The fourth rescue arrives in the same words as the others and then diverges. There is no closing name of God here, and no second deliverance from shame; the ayah moves directly from the saving to the sound and then to the aftermath. Commentators note the compression, which puts rescue and destruction inside one sentence and gives the final clause to the town rather than to the people who were spared.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Other accounts of Median describe the punishment differently, and classical commentators discuss the variation, generally reading the accounts as one event seen from different angles or as successive stages of it. This surah gives the version matching what it said of Thamud, reusing the same two words for the sound and the stillness.

keyTerms.note: The identical phrase closes each rescue in this surah. Naming mercy rather than merit every single time keeps the four deliverances from being read as rewards earned by whoever happened to survive.

A single cry, the same word used of Thamud earlier in this surah. The Quran gives Median more than one description of its ending across different chapters, and the commentators treat the accounts as compatible.
Bodies come to rest with their limbs beneath them, as a camel kneels. Repeating the exact word used of Thamud makes the two endings identical in a reader's mind, twenty-seven ayat apart.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An emptied settlement on a trade road told its own story. Caravans arriving to find houses standing and nobody inside them understood at once that whatever happened had been fast, since a town abandoned slowly is stripped first. The picture here, of people still in their own homes, described a scene travellers occasionally met and could not explain.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah closes four destructions and only one of them ends on names of God. Median's ends without any, moving straight from the mercy that saved Shuaib to the sound that took the town, and its final clause repeats word for word the phrase used of Thamud twenty-seven ayat earlier in the chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is named as the operative cause of every rescue in this surah, four times in identical words, and merit is never mentioned. That is a consistent position and it changes how the surviving groups should be read, since they are not being presented as people who earned an outcome. The repeated wording across four different peoples also makes the pattern the point rather than any single case.

crossReferences.why: Gives Median's end as a tremor instead, with Shuaib's parting words to the silent town.
Records the same mission and ending in two ayat, with the tremor seizing them in their homes.
Names the punishment of the day of gloom, another account of how the same people ended.

studies.applyIt: Four times in this chapter people are saved and the reason given is mercy, never their record. Think about the last narrow escape you had, the illness caught early, the accident that missed. You probably explained it by something you did. Try leaving that explanation out for a day and see whether anything actually changes.

studies.title: The Command Of Pharaoh
studies.meaning: One people is dismissed and the next narrative begins immediately, compressed almost to nothing. Moses is sent with signs and clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and everything that follows is given in a single observation: they followed Pharaoh's command, and that command was not sound. Commentators note that the surah spends three ayat on a story it tells at great length elsewhere, and read the brevity as deliberate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. By this point the chapter has given four extended narratives, and the account of Moses is placed fifth in a deliberately shortened form. Commentators read the compression as a signal that the pattern has been established, so the audience now supplies from the earlier accounts everything this one declines to spell out.

keyTerms.note: The noun means authority arising from proof rather than from force. Pairing it with signs distinguishes what Moses carried from the kind of command Pharaoh was exercising over the very same people.
The phrase is repeated twice inside one ayah, which is unusual and pointed. Naming the command rather than the man makes the failure a matter of what they obeyed rather than whom they admired.

The third and final occurrence of this word in the Quran, all three of them in this surah. Here it is denied of Pharaoh's command, having been sought in vain in a crowd and offered sarcastically to Shuaib.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt was the great neighbouring civilisation, known to Arabia through trade and through the older communities settled along the routes. Its ruler stood for centralised power of a kind no Arabian tribe possessed, where one man's word moved an entire country. Naming Pharaoh's command as the thing followed described an arrangement Arabians could see clearly precisely because they lived outside it.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah uses the word for sound judgement three times, and nowhere else in the Quran does it appear at all. Lot searches a crowd for one man who has it, Median offers it to Shuaib apparently in sarcasm, and here it is denied of Pharaoh's command. The chapter builds a small argument out of one word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the failure in following rather than in ruling. Pharaoh is named three times across two ayat and never once described; what gets described is his command and the people who took it up. That distributes the responsibility, and it matches the verdict passed earlier on Aad, who were likewise said to have followed the order of every obstinate tyrant.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same commission in the same words, with signs and a clear authority, to the same court.
States the outcome in a single line: Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them.
Records the arrival before Pharaoh and his dignitaries, and how the signs were actually received.

studies.applyIt: The failure named here is following an instruction that was not sound. Think of a rule you follow at work or at home that you have never assessed on its merits, only on who issued it. Assess it once this week. You may well keep it. The point is that you will then be following your own judgement.

studies.title: He Goes Before Them
studies.meaning: The image is of a leader at the head of a column, and the verb is the ordinary one for going in front. What he brings them to is described with a word from the desert: the arrival at water. Commentators note the bitterness of that choice, since the whole vocabulary here belongs to a guide bringing his people to a well after a long march. The last clause simply names what they find waiting there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators place this ayah as the answer to the one before it, where the people are said to have followed Pharaoh's command. Leadership in this world is extended into the next, so the arrangement they accepted does not end with them: the same man walks in front, and the destination is finally disclosed.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for preceding, used of a guide at the head of a travelling group. It carries no violence at all, which is what makes the ayah unsettling: the relationship simply continues as it was.
A word for arriving at a well or river to drink, and for the party that does so. Applying it to the Fire turns the desert's most welcome moment into its exact opposite.
The passive participle of the same root, so the phrase pairs the coming with the destination. That doubling gives the closing clause its weight in Arabic, and it occurs once in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reaching water was the shape of every journey in Arabia. A guide's competence was measured by whether he brought his party to a well before their supply ran out, and the arrival was the moment of relief the whole march had been organised around. Describing Pharaoh as leading his people to a watering place made the destination land before the word Fire arrived.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase closing this ayah pairs a word with its own passive participle, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis. The following ayah does exactly the same thing with a different root, calling what they receive a poor gift given. Both phrases occur once each in the Quran, and they sit in consecutive ayat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes leadership a continuing relationship rather than a temporary arrangement. Whoever went in front here goes in front there, which turns the question of whom you follow into a question about a destination rather than about a policy. It also declines to describe Pharaoh's punishment separately, since his position at the head of the column is itself the sentence.

crossReferences.why: Names them leaders calling to the Fire, who will not be helped on the Day of Resurrection.
Puts the same judgement in one line: Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them.
Shows those who were followed disowning their followers once the consequences become visible.

studies.applyIt: Being in front does not make someone a guide, and this ayah keeps the two apart. Think of one person whose lead you take in some area of life, and ask where the road they are on actually ends up. Not whether they are good company. Where the road goes. Those are different questions and we routinely confuse them.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Some Standing, Some Reaped
studies.meaning: The sentence on Pharaoh's people uses the construction this surah applied to Aad, a curse sent after them into both worlds. Then the narratives stop and the chapter looks back across all of them at once. The image is agricultural: of the towns just described, some are still upright and some have been cut down. Commentators note the tense, since both conditions are present now, and neither is offered as the more instructive of the two.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah closes the narrative section of the surah, which has run since the twenty-fifth ayah. Commentators read it as addressed to an audience that could travel to some of these sites and could not locate the others at all, which is precisely the distinction the closing image is drawing.

keyTerms.note: A noun paired with its own passive participle, a construction of emphasis. The word means a gift or assistance offered, so their curse is named in the vocabulary of hospitality. It occurs once.

The same word for significant news used earlier in this surah of the unseen. Here it is attached to towns rather than to hidden events, so the accounts are offered as history rather than as disclosure.
Two agricultural terms, used of a crop still upright and a crop already harvested. Applying them to towns compresses the whole preceding section into a farmer's glance across a field.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A harvested field was an ordinary sight and a startling one. Grain stood shoulder high one week and lay flat the next, and the ground that had been full was bare, with nothing broken or burned. Describing ruined civilisations as reaped rather than as destroyed gave the audience an image of an ending that arrives on schedule.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a harvested crop occurs four times in the Quran, and three of those describe destroyed peoples rather than actual fields.
