The metaphor is consistent across the Book: a community is a standing crop and its end is a harvest rather than a catastrophe, which is part of why these passages read as calm.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing image refuses to draw a moral. Some of the towns are still there and some are gone, and the ayah never says which condition indicates what, so the reader is left holding the fact of the difference rather than an explanation of it. That restraint runs right through the surah's narrative section, which has reported outcomes and left the arithmetic to whoever is listening.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same harvest image of this world's life, cut down as though it had never flourished.
Describes generations reaped with the same word, until they were made silent ashes.
Names the stilled wells and lofty mansions left behind, and asks whether they have travelled to look.

studies.applyIt: The ayah puts standing and reaped in the same glance without ranking them. Do that once today with two things in your own life, one that is still going and one that has finished. Look at them together rather than separately. The point is not melancholy. It is that both are the same kind of thing at different stages.

studies.title: They Wronged Themselves
studies.meaning: The verdict on all the preceding stories is given in one clause and it is an acquittal of God rather than a charge against the towns. Nothing was done to them that they had not done to themselves. Then the gods are audited: when the command arrived they added nothing, and the closing word says they added something after all, and it was ruin. Commentators note the irony, since what was invested in for protection turned out to be the multiplier of the loss.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the survey of the towns. Commentators read this ayah as the surah's own summary of its narrative section, forestalling a reading in which God is arbitrary and the peoples merely unlucky. The point is put before any of the remaining argument about the Day of Judgement begins.

keyTerms.note: The verb means putting a thing somewhere it does not belong. Applied reflexively, it describes people who mislocated themselves rather than people who were mistreated by somebody else.
The verb is about sufficing and making someone independent of need. Denying it of the gods states the failure precisely: they were kept for the moment of need, and at that moment they did nothing.
A verbal noun for destruction and diminishing, occurring only here in the Quran. Its position at the end of a sentence about adding nothing turns the clause around: they did add something after all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal god was an investment with running costs. Shrines were maintained, offerings made, and pilgrimages organised around them, and the outlay was justified by the protection expected in return. Auditing that arrangement at the moment of crisis was something merchants understood perfectly, since every partnership was eventually judged by what it returned when needed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for ruin that closes this ayah occurs only once in the whole Quran, and its root is rare across the Book, surfacing in just a handful of places. One of them opens a very short surah with the ruin of a man's two hands, and another says that all the scheming of Pharaoh came only to ruin.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage rules out a reading the narratives could easily have supported. Four peoples were destroyed, and the summary insists that the injury in each case was self-inflicted, which locates responsibility rather than distributing it. The audit of the gods then makes the same point from the other direction, since what a person relies on is tested by whether it is there at the one moment it was kept for.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle generally: God does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves.
Says of earlier peoples too that God did not wrong them, but they wronged their own selves.
Repeats the acquittal in the fewest possible words: We did them no injustice, they were the unjust.

studies.applyIt: Everybody keeps something for emergencies: a person they would call, a fund, a fallback plan. Ask what you would actually reach for if things went badly this month, and then ask honestly whether it would hold. This ayah is not asking you to abandon it. It is asking you to know what it is worth before you need it.

studies.title: Such Is His Grip
studies.meaning: One word carries the whole ayah, and it is a physical one: taking hold. This is how your Lord takes hold when He takes hold of towns that are doing wrong, and the clause specifies the timing, in the midst of the wrongdoing rather than afterwards. Two adjectives close it, painful and severe. Commentators note that nothing is described here except the manner of the seizure, which is what generalises the four stories just told.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and read by commentators as the point where the narratives are turned into a principle. Mecca's leadership had watched no such thing happen in living memory, and the surah's answer is not to predict one but to describe the character of the taking, which the four accounts have just illustrated in different forms.

keyTerms.note: The noun is the ordinary word for seizing or grasping something in the hand. Using it rather than a word for punishing keeps the emphasis on the manner of the act rather than on its justice.
A circumstantial clause fixing the timing. The town is taken while the wrongdoing is under way, not after it has stopped, which answers the assumption that a warning implies an interval.
Two adjectives with no conjunction between them, which intensifies rather than lists. The first names what it feels like and the second names its force, and Arabic packs both onto one noun.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seizure was a legal act in that world. A creditor could take a debtor's goods, a raiding party took what it could hold, and a chief seized a man against a claim, so the word carried the sense of something taken by right and without negotiation. Everyone listening had seen a seizure carried out and knew there was no appealing one.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names no people, no place and no event, which makes it unusual in a chapter otherwise packed with names. Sitting directly after the survey of the towns, it converts four particular histories into a single statement about how such things happen, using one verb of grasping and two adjectives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage holds fear and hope together by what it says and by where it sits. The description is severe and it is placed after four accounts in which believers were saved every time, by mercy and never by merit. Commentators read the pairing as the surah's method: the same God is described taking hold of towns and delivering the few, and both descriptions are meant to be carried at once.

crossReferences.why: Lists the different forms the taking took, sandstorm, blast, and the ground caving in beneath them.
Says that if He seized people for their wrongs at once, He would leave no creature moving on earth.
Makes the same point about deferral: He defers them to a stated term rather than seizing immediately.

studies.applyIt: Read this ayah and then read 16:61, which says that if wrongs were seized on immediately nothing living would be left. Hold the two together for a minute without resolving them. Most of us keep only one of these in mind at a time, and which one we keep tends to say more about our mood than about the truth.

studies.title: A Day To Be Witnessed
studies.meaning: The sign in all of this is offered to one kind of person, whoever fears the punishment of the hereafter, which narrows the audience rather than the evidence. Then the day is described twice in a single line: a day for which humanity is gathered, and a day that is witnessed. Commentators note the second phrase, since it says nothing about what happens and only that everyone will be present, with nobody watching from outside.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The resurrection was the point of hardest resistance in Mecca, and this surah has been arguing it since its seventh ayah. Here the argument is transferred from the histories just told, so what has been shown about towns is offered as evidence for a gathering, and the connection is left for the reader to make.

keyTerms.note: The condition is placed on the receiver rather than on the sign. Nothing about the evidence changes; what changes is whether a person is in a position to read it, which the ayah makes a matter of fear.
A passive construction: the gathering is done to them. The word for people is universal here, so the ayah describes an assembly with no category of persons left outside it.
A passive participle meaning both seen and attended in person. It occurs three times in the Quran, and it names the day by the fact of its audience rather than by anything that happens in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The great gatherings of Arabia were the pilgrimage seasons and the market fairs, when tribes normally at odds camped in one valley under a truce. Everyone came, disputes were suspended, and reputations were made and destroyed in public within days. A day described as gathered and attended used the largest social event those listeners knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing this day as witnessed occurs three times in the Quran, and the other two are strikingly ordinary by comparison. At 17:78 it describes the recitation at dawn as witnessed, and at 85:3 it appears in an oath, paired with the witness. The same participle covers a daily prayer and the final gathering.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making the sign available only to whoever fears the hereafter is a claim about how evidence works. The histories are equally visible to everyone, and what determines whether they signify is a prior disposition, which the passage names without apology. The description of the day then adds its own point: what makes it terrible is not primarily punishment but the fact that everyone is present for it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word of the dawn recitation, calling it witnessed, in a quite different setting.
Places the same participle in an oath, paired with the one who witnesses, at a surah's opening.
Shows the gathering itself, with jinn and humans assembled and answering for one another.

studies.applyIt: The sign here is only legible to someone already inclined to look. That is worth noticing about yourself: the things that persuade you usually find you already half-persuaded. Rather than arguing anyone into anything today, spend the argument on your own attention, and read one page of this surah as if you were being addressed.

studies.title: No Soul Will Speak
studies.meaning: Three short ayat cover the postponement, the arrival, and the division. The delay is given a number rather than a reason. Then on the day itself nobody speaks without permission, which removes the one thing every accused person expects to have. The division follows in two words, and the second of them is used nowhere else in the Quran. Commentators note that the wretched are described first and at greater length.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demand to have the punishment brought forward runs through this surah from its eighth ayah, and here it is finally answered in the plainest terms: the delay has a fixed count attached. Commentators read the sequence as closing the argument the chapter opened with, before it turns to what the two groups receive.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means numbered rather than merely appointed. It concedes the delay while insisting the count exists and is held elsewhere, which is the answer to every demand for haste in this surah.
The verb is of ordinary talking rather than of pleading. Removing speech itself, before any question of defence arises, is what makes the scene silent rather than merely unfavourable.
Two nouns dividing everyone into two groups. The second occurs only here in the Quran in this form, which is striking given how common its root is in later Arabic naming.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Speech was how justice worked in Arabia. A man defended himself in front of the assembly, and his eloquence, his witnesses and his standing were what he had; a dispute was won by whoever spoke best. Describing a court where nobody speaks without permission removed the entire instrument that free men relied on to protect themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the fortunate in this passage occurs only once in the Quran, here. Its opposite, the word for the wretched, is used ten times across the Book. The pairing of the two, dividing all of humanity into exactly two named groups, happens in this ayah and nowhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a demand for haste with a number rather than a justification, which is consistent with the surah's refusal to let the delay be read as absence. Then it removes speech, and the effect is to strip away the last thing a person could bring. What remains is the division itself, stated without any account of how it was arrived at, and left standing at the end of the ayah.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same silence: they will not speak except whoever the Merciful permits, and speaks rightly.
Says intercession will not avail except for one whom the Merciful permits and whose word He accepts.
Answers the same demand for haste, saying the matter between us would have been settled already.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your anxiety about being judged is really about not being able to explain yourself. Most of us rehearse defences constantly, for conversations that never happen. Pick one such rehearsal today and let it go unfinished, deliberately. You will find the situation itself is unchanged, and you are carrying less of it.

studies.title: Except As Your Lord Wills
studies.meaning: Duration is stated and then qualified in the same breath. They remain as long as the heavens and the earth last, which fixes the term to the largest thing available, and then an exception is attached: except what your Lord wills. Commentators have written extensively on that clause and offer several readings without agreeing. The closing phrase then explains why it is there, naming God as one who does whatever He intends.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical commentaries treat this ayah and the one following it together, since both carry the same duration and the same exception. The discussion in the tradition is long and unresolved, and the major commentators set out the range of interpretations rather than establishing one, which is itself worth noticing about a passage of this weight.

keyTerms.gloss: as long as the heavens last
keyTerms.note: An Arabic idiom for permanence, using the most durable thing a speaker could name. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah, in consecutive ayat about opposite destinations.
An exception clause attached to a stated permanence. Commentators read it in several ways and none is agreed, so the classical sources record the range and let the sentence keep its reservation.
An intensive form of the word for one who acts, so the sense is a constant doer rather than one who acted once. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times closing a statement about outcomes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic swore permanence by what was visibly permanent. A man promised something for as long as the stars turn, or as long as a mountain stands, and everyone understood the formula as meaning without end rather than as an actual measurement. Attaching an exception to such a formula was unusual, and it was the sort of qualification a careful contract would carry.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase closing this ayah, describing God as one who does what He intends, occurs twice in the Quran. The other is at 85:16, where it likewise ends a passage about severe consequence, and both times it stands immediately after a name or an act of mercy has been mentioned rather than before it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah asserts a term and then declines to close it, which is unusual for a passage of this seriousness. Commentators have used the exception in more than one direction and the tradition has not settled the question, so the honest position is that the clause is there and its scope is disputed. What the closing phrase establishes is that no outcome constrains the one who decided it.

crossReferences.why: Carries the identical duration and the identical exception, applied to the opposite destination.
Uses the same closing phrase, that He is the doer of whatever He intends, after severe warning.
Describes the same destination as a place of remaining for ages, using a similarly open measure.

studies.applyIt: This is a passage where the classical scholars did not reach agreement, and the honest response is to hold it as they did. Practise that once today on something smaller: a question about your own life you have been forcing to a conclusion. Say to yourself that you do not know, and notice that the not knowing is bearable.

studies.title: A Gift Never Cut Off
studies.meaning: The second half of the division is given in the same shape as the first, with the same duration and the same reservation attached. What differs is the final phrase, which the other ayah does not have. A gift that is never severed, and the word used is from cutting rather than from ending. Commentators note that the reservation is answered here by a guarantee, so the sentence closes on continuation rather than on an open question.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators treat this ayah alongside the one before it, since the two are built identically and describe opposite outcomes. The addition at the end of this one is where the classical discussion concentrates, and the majority read it as removing any suggestion that the reservation could mean interruption of the reward.

keyTerms.note: A passive form: they were made happy rather than becoming so by themselves. The construction quietly attributes the outcome to somebody else, matching the way this surah has described every rescue.

The word is for something given freely rather than owed, which is a different category from a wage. It reframes the whole description that precedes it, since gifts are measured by the giver rather than the work.

A passive participle from a root meaning to sever or lop, occurring only here in the Quran. Denying it makes continuity an assurance rather than an assumption, and answers the reservation just stated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in Arabian life was uninterrupted. Wells failed, palms were cut, alliances lapsed and grazing moved with the rain, and even a generous patron's support ended when he died or was defeated. A gift described as never severed was describing the one quality every arrangement in that world lacked, which is why the word chosen is one of cutting.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for never cut off occurs once in the whole Quran. Its root is the ordinary one for lopping a branch or severing a rope, so the assurance is phrased in the vocabulary of orchards and tents rather than in abstract terms about time. It is the last word of the ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the reward a gift changes its logic. The passage has just described people who were made fortunate, in a passive construction, and it now calls what they receive a bestowal rather than a wage, which removes the transaction from the picture entirely. The final phrase then supplies the assurance the previous ayah withheld, and the asymmetry between the two is deliberate.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same duration and the same reservation, applied to the opposite destination, without this assurance.
Describes abundant fruit there as neither cut off nor withheld from those who reach it.
Calls the provision there Our provision, for which there is no exhausting at all.

studies.applyIt: The one thing described here that nothing in this life has is uninterruptedness. Notice today how much of your worry is really about continuity: whether the job holds, whether the health holds, whether the person stays. That worry is accurate about this world. Let this ayah name the single place where it does not apply.

studies.title: Only As Their Fathers Did
studies.meaning: The instruction is not to be uncertain about what these people worship, and the reason given is genealogical rather than theological. They worship exactly as their fathers worshipped before them, so what looks like conviction is inheritance running forward under its own momentum. Commentators note the closing clause, which promises them their full share without any reduction, and read it as covering both what they are owed and what is coming to them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The appeal to ancestral practice is the objection recorded from three of the peoples in this surah and from Mecca itself, and here the chapter names it directly. Commentators read the instruction as addressed to the Prophet, steadying him against the impression that a long-established practice must rest on something.

keyTerms.note: The noun means a wavering uncertainty rather than a considered disagreement. The instruction is against being unsettled by what they do, which is a different thing from being told what to believe about it.
The comparison is of manner, not merely of object. What is inherited is described as the whole practice, so the resemblance covers the reasons and the assumptions as well as the rites.
A passive participle from the verb to diminish, the same root used earlier in this surah of shortening a measure. The commercial vocabulary returns here, applied to what these people finally receive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Arabia was transmitted like property. A family kept a particular idol, a clan maintained a shrine, and the practices came down intact with the obligations attached to them, so a man's worship was as inherited as his name and his grazing rights. Nobody in that world chose a religion; they received one, and were expected to hand it on.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for reduction that closes this ayah comes from the same root as the verb used at 11:85, where Median are told not to shortchange people of their belongings. The chapter uses one commercial root for a fraud committed in a market and for a settlement that will be paid out in full.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage explains a practice without excusing it. Inheritance accounts for why people worship as they do, and the ayah offers that as an explanation, but the closing clause still delivers each person their full portion, so the account of the cause does not cancel the consequence. Commentators read the two halves as deliberately held together rather than as one qualifying the other.

crossReferences.why: Records the same defence, that we follow what we found our fathers on, and its answer.
Gives the identical reply across peoples: we found our parents on a course and follow their footsteps.
Asks whether they would follow their fathers even if the devil were calling them to the Fire.

studies.applyIt: Pick one religious habit you have and trace where you got it: a parent, a teacher, a place. This is not an argument against it, since almost everything worth having comes to us that way. The exercise is to know which of your practices you have actually examined and which you have only received, and to be honest about the ratio.

studies.title: A Word That Went Before
studies.meaning: A scripture was given and disagreement followed it, which is stated as a fact rather than as a complaint. What prevented the dispute from being settled at the time was a prior word from God, and commentators read that as the decision to defer judgement to an appointed day rather than to resolve arguments as they arise. Then the second ayah promises each party full payment, using the merchant's verb the surah has used throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and read by commentators as consolation. A community facing entrenched disagreement in Mecca is shown that the earlier scripture met the same fate, and that the continuing argument is not evidence of a failure. The Book of Moses is invoked here as it was near the surah's opening, framing the whole chapter between two references to it.

keyTerms.note: A passive construction, so no party is named as the one who caused the split. The grammar keeps the ayah descriptive, reporting that disagreement happened rather than assigning it to anyone.
A decision already issued, described as having gone ahead of events. The phrase occurs five times in the Quran and always explains why a matter that could be closed has been left open.

keyTerms.gloss: He will surely pay in full
keyTerms.note: An emphatic form of the verb for settling an account completely. The commercial vocabulary running through this surah reappears at its close, applied to what every person finally receives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in that world could run for generations without resolution, and everyone accepted that some matters simply waited. A claim over a well or a killing might be held open for years by agreement, with both parties knowing an eventual reckoning was coming, because there was no authority above them who could settle it sooner. Deferral was a familiar condition, not a failure.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah appears almost word for word at 41:45, where the same scripture is given, the same dispute follows, and the same prior word prevents the matter from being closed. The two passages are among the closest verbatim parallels in the Quran, sitting in chapters revealed to answer the same objections.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Disagreement is presented as expected rather than as a failure of revelation. That reframes the position of a small community surrounded by rejection, since the argument continuing is exactly what a prior decision to defer would produce. Full payment for each person then supplies what deferral withholds, so nothing is being cancelled by the delay, only postponed to where it can be settled properly.

crossReferences.why: Gives nearly the same sentence: the Book of Moses given, disputed, and judgement deferred by a prior word.
Says humanity was one community and then differed, held open by the same prior decree.
Adds the reason for the split: it came after knowledge arrived, out of rivalry among themselves.

studies.applyIt: Some disagreements are not going to be resolved, and treating them as though they should be is its own kind of exhaustion. Identify one in your life that you have been trying to close for years. Try holding it open deliberately for a month instead. Not conceding, not winning: just no longer requiring it to finish.

studies.title: Be Upright As Commanded
studies.meaning: The command is to stand straight, and two qualifications are attached at once. It is to be done as you were commanded, which fixes the standard outside the person. And it takes in those who turned back alongside him. Then a ban on going beyond. Early scholars read that as the particular danger of uprightness, since somebody correcting their course tends to overcorrect. The closing clause is about being seen rather than about reward.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah that has recounted one destroyed community after another. It also names the prophets sent to warn them. After all that history the instruction turns personal. Classical sources preserve a report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) found this verse among the most demanding addressed to him. Early scholars return to it when discussing what uprightness costs.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to stand that means holding a straight line, used of a road without bends. It asks for a direction maintained over time rather than for a single correct act.
From a root for water rising past its banks and for tyranny. It names going beyond a boundary, and its use here warns that zeal has the same shape as the flood it means to prevent.
The same verb used of repentance throughout the Quran. Describing the community as those who turned back with him defines them by a movement they made rather than by a status they hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel depended on holding a line. A caravan that drifted a few degrees off course over a day's march could miss a well by miles, and guides were valued for keeping direction across ground with no landmarks at all. Correction was constant and small. The vocabulary of staying straight was practical language about survival long before it was ever moral language.
studies.didYouKnow: The command in this verse is singular and the ban that follows is plural, which the classical grammarians point out. One man is told to stand straight. Then a whole group is told not to overstep. So the sentence moves from an individual instruction to a warning for everyone inside a single line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Uprightness is defined by an outside standard rather than by sincerity. That is the work the phrase about being commanded does. It stops the straight path from becoming whatever a person's own conscience produces. The warning against excess then guards the other flank. The danger to someone trying to be upright is not usually slackness but zeal. And the sentence closes with seeing rather than with threat.

crossReferences.why: Describes what comes to those who said our Lord is God and then stood straight.
Gives the same command with an instruction not to follow their desires.
Follows immediately, warning against inclining towards those who do wrong.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have been doing well recently and check it for overcorrection. The early night that became a rule you enforce on everyone. The budget that has made you tight rather than careful. The verse puts its warning about excess directly after the command to be straight, and it does so for a reason.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to keep going straight, just as he was told to, and those who turned back with him too. He warns them not to go too far. God sees everything they do.

studies.title: Do Not Lean Towards Them
studies.meaning: The verb chosen is the mildest one available and that is the whole point. Do not lean towards those who do wrong, which describes an inclination rather than an alliance, a slight shift of weight rather than a decision. Commentators note the strength of what follows such a small movement: the Fire touching, and then the absence of any protector. What is being warned against is proximity of sympathy, not participation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and placed among the surah's closing instructions. The community around the Prophet was under pressure to soften its position for the sake of getting along in a small city where everyone was a neighbour or a relative. Commentators read the ayah in that setting rather than as a general rule about association.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a supporting pillar, so the verb means to lean on something or to incline towards it. It occurs once in the Quran, and its mildness is what gives the warning its force.

keyTerms.gloss: and the Fire would touch you
keyTerms.note: The verb of touching, not of burning or seizing. It matches the smallness of the leaning, so a slight inclination is answered by a slight contact rather than by an overwhelming one.
The plural of a word for a close ally who defends you. Denying that any exist besides God removes the practical benefit that inclining towards the powerful is supposed to secure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in Mecca depended on somebody. Trade needed partners, safety needed a clan, and a marriage tied families that might otherwise be at odds, so leaning towards the influential was not a moral failure but the ordinary way of surviving. This instruction cut into a network of small accommodations that nobody thought of as choices at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb here occurs only once in the Quran, and its root appears earlier in this same surah at 11:80, where Lot wishes he had a strong pillar to lean on. The chapter uses one image twice: a prophet longing for something to lean on, and its readers told not to lean where they are tempted to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the danger at the beginning rather than at the end of a process. Nothing is said about joining wrongdoers or approving of them, only about inclining, which is where such things actually start and where they are still easy to stop. The clause about protectors then removes the calculation, since what inclination is usually purchasing turns out not to be available.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root, where Lot wishes for a strong pillar he could have leaned on.
Describes pressure to incline slightly towards them, and how nearly it succeeded.
Names the wish behind such pressure: they would like you to compromise, so they could compromise.

studies.applyIt: Leaning is the word to notice. Not agreeing with something you know is wrong, just letting your weight settle slightly towards it: laughing along, staying vague, not correcting an impression. Catch yourself doing that once this week and simply stand up straight instead. You do not have to say anything. The correction is postural.

studies.title: At Both Ends Of The Day
studies.meaning: Times are given rather than a number: the two ends of the day, and the stretches of night that draw near to them. Then a statement about how good deeds work on bad ones. It uses a verb for taking something away. Early scholars read the prayer named just before as the leading instance of that. The passage closes with patience and a promise that no reward for doing well is lost. So the sequence runs from a fixed practice to a long endurance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah full of peoples that were wiped out. The instruction arrives straight after that list of endings. Early scholars read the placement as chosen with care. The answer to a long account of collapse is a timetable. A widely told report connects the verse with a man who came to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after doing something he regretted, and was told this.

keyTerms.note: A dual form for the two edges of something. Naming the day by its ends rather than by hours gives times anyone can find without an instrument, at the boundaries where the light changes.
From a root for approaching and for closeness. It names the parts of the night nearest to the day, so the times given cluster around the transitions rather than around the middle of anything.
A causative verb meaning to make something go. The good deeds are its subject and the bad ones its object, so the removal is described as an action the deeds themselves perform.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was told by light. Work began when a white thread could be told from a black one and ended when the sun went down; travellers timed departures by first light and rested at midday. Nobody owned a clock. Fixing devotion to the edges of daylight tied it to the two moments everyone in a settlement already noticed and organised their day around.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that good deeds take away bad ones is among the most quoted half-sentences in the Quran. In the Arabic, the verb has the good deeds acting on the bad rather than a person acting on either. The grammar keeps the agency with the deeds. Classical scholars point that out when discussing how the removal is understood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Regret is given something to do. Instead of prescribing a feeling, the passage supplies a schedule. It places that schedule at the boundaries of a day, so the whole day sits between two fixed points. The claim about good deeds then explains why the schedule matters. The closing instruction to be patient adds the missing dimension. This works over a length of time rather than in a moment.

crossReferences.why: Fixes prayer to the sun's decline and the dawn, adding a portion of the night.
Gives similar times, before sunrise and before setting and during the night.
Describes those who are patient and establish prayer as repelling evil with good.

studies.applyIt: Choose one of the two edges of the day, morning or evening, and put a small fixed act there for a week. Two minutes of recitation, one page, a set of words you say. Not both ends, one. The verse anchors devotion to a boundary that arrives whether or not you are ready, and that is the useful part of it.
studies.explainEasier: Pray at both ends of the day and in the near parts of the night. Good things you do take away the bad. Keep going and be patient, because God never loses the reward of people who do good.

studies.title: People With Something Left
studies.meaning: The question is put as a regret about history rather than as an accusation. Why were there not, among the generations before you, people with something left in them who forbade corruption in the land. A few were, and they were saved. Then the diagnosis: the wrongdoers went after the luxuries they had been given to enjoy. Commentators read the passage as naming comfort itself as what silenced the objectors who should have existed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's closing section after the narratives are complete. The word for those given comfort recurs across the Quran in accounts of destroyed towns, where the affluent are consistently the first to reject a warner. Commentators read this ayah as generalising what the four narratives have each shown in a particular form.

keyTerms.note: The noun means a remainder, and commentators read it as remaining understanding, remaining virtue, or remaining strength of judgement. The same root appears earlier in this surah, of what God leaves you.
The participle is continuous: people who go on forbidding rather than who object once. What is regretted is the absence of a standing practice, not the absence of a single brave protest.
A passive verb from a root meaning to be softened by ease. The Quran uses this root of affluent classes in destroyed towns, and this particular form occurs only here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's leading families had grown rich on the caravan trade within living memory, and comfort of that kind was recent enough to be visible. Imported goods, larger houses, and the leisure to argue about religion at all marked the men who ran the city. The ayah describes a mechanism they would have recognised in their own fathers' rise.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those made comfortable occurs in this exact form only here in the Quran, though its root recurs across accounts of destroyed towns. At 34:34 the pattern is stated flatly: no warner was ever sent to any town without its affluent being the ones who rejected what he brought.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah shifts responsibility from the wrongdoers to the people who should have objected and did not. That is an unusual place to put the weight, and commentators note it: a society is judged by whether it produced anyone still capable of saying no. Naming comfort as the cause then makes the failure ordinary rather than wicked, which is what makes the ayah uncomfortable.

crossReferences.why: States the pattern outright: no warner came to a town without its affluent rejecting his message.
Records who was saved in an earlier case: those who had been forbidding the wrong.
Names the failure precisely: they did not restrain one another from the wrongs they committed.

studies.applyIt: The people missing from this ayah are not heroes; they are ordinary people who would still say something. Being comfortable makes that quietly harder, because objecting has a cost and comfort is what you would be risking. Notice one thing this week you have not mentioned because it would be awkward, and mention it.

studies.title: One Community, Had He Willed
studies.meaning: Two statements sit together and each limits the other. Towns are not destroyed while their people are putting things right, which makes conduct rather than belief the operative condition in that sentence. Then a different claim entirely: uniformity was available and was not chosen, and they go on differing. Commentators note the tense of the last verb, which is continuous, so the differing is presented as an ongoing condition rather than a past event.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's closing argument after four destroyed peoples have been described. Commentators read the first of these ayat as forestalling a conclusion the narratives might invite, that destruction falls on communities arbitrarily. The second then addresses the deeper question of why disagreement exists at all, which the chapter has been circling since its opening.

keyTerms.note: The participle is from the root for repair and soundness, the same one behind the word for good deeds. It describes an activity rather than a belief, which is what makes this condition specific.
The phrase appears nine times in the Quran, usually in exactly this construction about what could have been. It names uniformity as an available option that was deliberately not taken.

A continuous participle rather than a past verb, so the differing is a standing condition. The root covers both disagreement and variety, and the classical commentators discuss which sense carries here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia was a patchwork by nature. Tribes kept different gods, different dialects, different calendars and different customs of marriage and revenge, and unity was something achieved briefly for a pilgrimage or a war and then lost again. To that audience the idea that everyone might have been one community was not an ideal but an obvious impossibility.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about being made one community occurs nine times in the Quran, and in most of them it is a hypothetical that God declined: had He willed, He could have made you one. The Book returns to the same sentence repeatedly, and each time human difference is presented as chosen rather than as a failure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first ayah puts a limit on destruction that has nothing to do with creed, since a town of people repairing things is not destroyed. The second makes plurality deliberate. Together they change how the four narratives should be read, since none of those towns was ruined for holding a different view; each was ruined while a practice was under way that its own people were no longer willing to stop.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same statement about one congregation, followed by responsibility for what you did.
Repeats it and adds that He admits into His mercy whomever He wills among the differing.
Says humanity was one community and then differed, held open by a word that went before.

studies.applyIt: Uniformity was available and was not taken. That is worth carrying into a disagreement this week, particularly one where you catch yourself wishing everyone simply saw it your way. Difference is not the problem being solved here; it is the arrangement. Try acting for one conversation as though that were literally true.

studies.title: For That He Created Them
studies.meaning: An exception is made to the differing just described, and then a clause the classical tradition has debated for centuries: and for that He created them. Commentators read the pronoun as pointing back to mercy, so that mercy is the purpose of creation, and others read it as pointing to the differing itself. Both readings are recorded in the major commentaries. The ayah then closes with a decree already settled, quoted directly.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators treat this ayah alongside the one before it, since the exception it opens with only makes sense as a continuation. The disagreement over the pronoun is old and remains unresolved in the classical sources, which set the readings out beside one another rather than choosing between them.

keyTerms.gloss: except those He has shown mercy
keyTerms.note: The exception names a recipient rather than a quality, exactly as in the earlier ayah about the flood. Mercy is again the sole thing that distinguishes one group, and no other criterion is supplied.

keyTerms.gloss: and for that He created them
keyTerms.note: A demonstrative whose reference is disputed. Commentators read it as pointing to mercy or to the differing just mentioned, and the classical sources record both without settling the question.
The verb means being finished and whole. Applied to a decree it says the decision is closed rather than pending, which is why the sentence that follows can be quoted directly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A chief's word, once given publicly, was binding on him and on his people, and going back on it cost more than keeping it. Arabs distinguished carefully between an intention stated and a word completed, and only the second created an obligation. Saying that God's word is complete used a category everyone understood as final.
studies.didYouKnow: The declaration quoted at the end of this ayah appears four times in the Quran, at 7:18, here, 32:13 and 38:85. In three of those places it is addressed to Satan directly, and only here is it given as a completed word of the Lord within an argument about why humanity differs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts a disputed clause at the centre of the largest question the surah raises, and the tradition has not resolved it. What is not in dispute is the shape of the sentence: mercy is the exception to a universal condition, and it is named as a recipient rather than as something earned. The quoted decree then closes the chapter's argument on a note that is settled and not soft.

crossReferences.why: Gives creation a different purpose clause, worship, which commentators read alongside this one.
Quotes the same completed declaration, after saying He could have given every soul its guidance.
Places the same words at the very beginning of the human story, spoken as a sentence of expulsion.

studies.applyIt: This is the ayah in the surah where the classical scholars most openly disagree, and they wrote that down rather than smoothing it over. Try that once this week with something you are asked about and do not know: say that there are two views and you hold neither firmly. It is a harder sentence than it sounds.

studies.title: To Make Your Heart Firm
studies.meaning: The surah states its own purpose, and the purpose is emotional rather than informational. All of this narration is here to steady your heart. Three things are then said to have arrived with it, and they are distributed: the truth to the one receiving it, and a lesson and a reminder for the believers. Then the chapter hands him the formula it gave Shuaib earlier, and closes on waiting, which both sides turn out to be doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is one of the few places where the Quran says directly what a stretch of narrative is for, and commentators treat it as the key to reading the whole chapter. The instruction that follows is given to a man with no power to compel anybody, which is why it ends in mutual waiting rather than in any kind of threat.

keyTerms.note: The verb is of steadying something so it does not shift, used of feet on loose ground and of a heart under strain. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times of strengthening the Prophet through revelation.
A word for the heart as the seat of feeling and burning rather than of thought. Choosing it over the commoner term makes the effect of these stories emotional before it is doctrinal.
The same phrase Shuaib used to Median earlier in this surah. Handing it now to the Prophet places him where the narratives have been standing, at the end of an argument that talking cannot settle.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan waited out a sandstorm and a besieged settlement waited out a siege, and in both cases the waiting was the work itself. Arabic had a rich vocabulary for it, and everyone understood that outlasting was frequently the only available form of winning. Ending a long chapter with two parties both waiting described a familiar and exhausting condition.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for making the heart firm occurs twice in the Quran, and both concern the Prophet. Here it names the purpose of this surah's entire narrative section, and at 25:32 it explains why the revelation came down in stages rather than all at once. In both places the steadying is the stated reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the purpose changes how the preceding hundred ayat should be read. They are not primarily historical instruction or a warning aimed at opponents; they are addressed to somebody who needed them, and the surah says so plainly. That makes revelation partly a response to a person's condition, and it makes reading these accounts an activity with an intended effect rather than a source of facts.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb: the recitation came in stages precisely in order to strengthen your heart.
Says the same of another long narrative: in their stories is a lesson for people of understanding.
Ends a similar exchange the same way: so wait, and I am waiting here alongside you.

studies.applyIt: This chapter tells you what it is for. Read one of its prophet narratives, anywhere from the twenty-fifth ayah onward, not to learn something but to see whether it steadies you. That is a different kind of reading and it wants a slower pace. Notice at the end whether anything in you sits differently than it did.

studies.title: Worship Him And Rely
studies.meaning: The chapter closes by placing the unseen and the whole command with God, and then draws two consequences addressed to a person rather than to an argument: worship Him, rely on Him. Commentators note that these are the two things the surah has been asking for since its second ayah. The final clause then quietly changes the subject, from what God holds to what the reader is doing right now.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators observe that the surah ends where it started. Its second ayah stated that you should worship none but God, and its last says worship Him and rely on Him, so the whole chapter, with its five prophets and its four ruined towns, is enclosed between the same instruction given twice.

keyTerms.note: Whatever is absent from perception across the whole creation. Assigning it to God at the close answers the demands for signs and treasures that this chapter recorded near its opening.
A passive with the definite article, so it is the command or the affair as such rather than any particular one. The grammar leaves the returning under way rather than merely promised.
From the word for an agent entrusted with your business, the same term applied to God near this surah's opening. The imperative closes the chapter by asking for what Hud had already demonstrated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ending an address by naming what the listener owes was standard in Arabic oratory. A speech delivered at a gathering closed on the practical consequence rather than on the argument, and audiences expected the final line to tell them what to do next. This chapter follows that form exactly, giving two imperatives and a single observation as its close.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase closing this surah's instruction, worship Him and rely on Him, occurs once in the whole Quran. The chapter's second ayah opens with worship none but God, so its first instruction and its last are the same one, with a hundred and twenty ayat of prophet narratives standing between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ending is practical rather than triumphant. Having described four destroyed peoples and a day on which nobody speaks, the chapter closes by asking one person for two things, both ordinary and both available immediately. The final clause about God's awareness is then not a threat in this position but the reason those two instructions are worth acting on at all.

crossReferences.why: Closes a comparable argument with the same instruction, so worship Him, He is Guardian of everything.
States the same possession of the unseen, and adds how near the coming of the Hour is.
Ends another chapter with the same observation, that your Lord is not heedless of what you do.

studies.applyIt: Read the second ayah of this surah and then this one, back to back, and notice that they say the same thing. Everything in between is the argument for it. If you have been reading this chapter over the past while, let today's response be the small one it actually asks for: one act of worship, and one thing handed over.
